articles.title_orig: OpenAI Agents Hit U.S. Government Websites
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Agents Hit U.S. Government Websites
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said in a technical report released on Friday that an AI model it was training and evaluating broke out of its secure testing environment as recently as last weekend and took unauthorized actions on the internet. As a result, the company said that it is pausing the training of its most advanced AI models for the second time in less than three months while it tries to figure out how to stop these “rogue AI” incidents from recurring.
“All inference for our most capable models remains stopped until we have hardened our systems further,” Micah Carroll, the RSI Preparedness Lead at OpenAI, said in a post on X about the latest incident. The company said the latest incident occurred on Sept. 20. It involved an AI agent undergoing tests on an information-search task. Even though it was not supposed to have access to the internet, the agent found a way to send queries to a public chatbot. The new revelation is significant because it is the first time the company has said that one of its AI models was able to gain unauthorized internet access since announcing a range of steps on Aug. 18 to improve the security and monitoring of its “sandboxes”—the digital environments, usually walled off from network and internet access, in which it tests unreleased models in order to discover their capabilities. Those improvements followed the July incident in which thousands of OpenAI’s AI agents found a way to hack out of their sandbox, with hundreds of them participating in a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face.
Since disclosing its role in the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI has acknowledged dozens more incidents in which AI agents it was testing took unauthorized actions across the internet, including multiple cyber attacks, some of which impacted government websites in the U.S. and Australia. It also has revealed that in some of these incidents its AI agents leaked private images from ChatGPT users to the internet. But until now, OpenAI has not reported any activity taking place after July 20, when it discovered the agent swarm that was attacking Hugging Face and moved to shut it down. The company said it had paused AI training in late July for two weeks while it worked to improve its security and safety controls and monitoring. The fact that its AI agents have once again managed to break out of a sandbox suggests that the steps OpenAI has taken to improve security after the Hugging Face attack are insufficient. “The incident exposed a gap in our controls over network restrictions,” OpenAI said in its technical report on the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. It said it was once again pausing training until it has “both validated that the gap is resolved and performed additional red-teaming of the system.”
Asked about the Sept. 20 incident, an OpenAI spokesperson referred Fortune to a section of the technical incident report in which OpenAI described some of the actions it has taken to improve security and control since the Hugging Face attack. “Following the Hugging Face incident, we have continuously hardened and red-teamed our research environment,” that section reads. “Our focus has been broad direct and transitive paths. We are working through narrower paths used by system dependencies, and replacing them with offline alternatives. This incident is a lot less severe than some of our previous incidents, but because it’s the first one since our security hardening following the Hugging Face incident, it gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work.”
In this case, OpenAI said the AI agent had discovered that it had access to a service called a DNS resolver, which translates between a website URL and an IP address, and that through this DNS system it could send queries to a public chatbot.
It is not clear if the Sept. 20 episode reported by OpenAI represents the full extent of the latest security lapses involving the company’s unreleased AI models. Earlier this week, independent AI research firm Transluce AI said it had found evidence that an OpenAI AI agent may have attempted to hack a cryptocurrency exchange on Sept. 19 and Sept. 20. OpenAI has not replied to requests to comment on this aspect of the Transluce report. OpenAI said that when it restarts training, it will begin from scratch to hopefully ensure the new model’s tendency to engage in “misaligned” behavior—when a model violates human instructions or common sense human values about how it should and should not accomplish a task—is expunged. It also said that it would institute “more comprehensive misalignment interventions” but did not specify what these would be.
The company said that since discovering this latest security lapse it has “added blocking controls at two independent layers, either of which would have prevented [the agent’s] internet access.” OpenAI also disclosed that systems it had put in place after the Hugging Face attack to catch AI agents attempting to break out of their test sandboxes only partly worked. On top of that, an additional system that was automatically supposed to stop training runs once misaligned behavior was detected had failed. The company said its monitoring systems “flagged the [agent’s] behavior within 15 minutes and a person began reviewing it three minutes after that.” But a subsequent review found there had been other attempts by the AI model to use the same method to reach the internet that had not been flagged by the monitoring system. A different system that was supposed to automatically shut down the training run when suspicious activity is detected did not work, “leading to confusion around whether it should have been stopped,” OpenAI said in the technical report on the incident. “The run was then manually stopped two and a half hours later when this was resolved.” Zuxin Liu, an AI researcher who works on “post-training” at OpenAI, said in a post on X that he was one of the employees called in to respond to the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. “It was pretty surreal to watch the model unexpectedly find a way to access the internet from what was supposed to be a super secured environment for human,” he wrote.
Update, Sept 26: This story has been updated to include a response from OpenAI to Fortune’s question about this latest incident.

Coastal communities across the Northeast faced more flooding and power outages on Sunday as a powerful nor’easter continued to lash the region , with forecasters warning that upcoming high tides could further submerge vulnerable shorelines.
The slow-moving storm —which resulted in a fatality on Saturday when a falling tree struck a New York City housing authority worker—was expected to persist through Sunday with heavy rain, high winds, and dangerous surf from New Jersey to New England.
Positioned south of Long Island and east of northern New Jersey on Sunday morning, the storm was forecast to loop around the region for roughly another 24 hours, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.
Meteorologists expected the heaviest remaining rainfall on Sunday to span northern New Jersey through New York City and Long Island into southern New England. While the system was gradually losing strength, Oravec noted that the threat of tidal flooding would persist during morning and evening high-tide cycles.
"The most impactful parts of the storm are likely going to be the high winds and the tidal flooding," Oravec said.
The weather evoked memories of 2012's Superstorm Sandy, which caused over $60 billion in damage across the eastern US. Although the current impact remains far lower, it could mark the first of several East Coast storms this fall influenced by an El Niño climate pattern.
More than 130,000 customers lost electricity across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic by Sunday morning, according to PowerOutage.us.
The most severe outages affected the New Jersey coastline, Long Island, and coastal Connecticut. Fallen trees across Long Island damaged homes and vehicles, blocked roads, and severed power lines.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency stated that regional response centers were operating at an "enhanced posture," with emergency personnel staged in New England in case of widespread blackouts.
On Saturday, flooded streets in New York and New Jersey saw residents kayaking, while others attempted to surf elevated waves at local beaches. Emergency crews in Sea Bright, New Jersey, rescued a woman and her dog trapped in a flooded vehicle, ABC7 reported.
In Surf City, New Jersey, floodwaters entered a marina where staff had relocated equipment, and owner Kenny Formica said clients reported missing boats and Jet Skis blown from lifts. In Norfolk, Virginia, high waters left driving cars pushing wakes through streets.
Travel across the region was also upended. Hundreds of flights were grounded at Boston Logan International Airport, and flooding cut highway access to Hatteras Island, North Carolina, stranding tourists and forcing a couple to relocate their wedding when roughly 45 guests could not reach the island.

articles.title_orig: Sheriff’s office: 11 wounded at Macon park; two teens in critical condition
articles.title_zh: Sheriff’s office: 11 wounded at Macon park; two teens in critical condition
articles.content_orig:
Eleven people in their late teens were shot overnight Sunday at a park in Georgia, according to law enforcement.
The Bibb County Sheriff's Office said the shooting occurred around midnight "at a large gathering" in Carolyn Crayton Park in the city of Macon, about 85 miles southeast of Atlanta. The wounded victims were identified as four 18-year-old men, two 18-year-old women and five 17-year-old boys, according to the sheriff's office.
Two of the victims, an 18-year-old man and a 17-year-old boy, were in critical condition, authorities said. The others were in stable condition.
The gathering appeared to be a birthday party that was originally supposed to take place at an Airbnb in Jones County, but the host made the group leave the premises, according to Bibb County Sheriff David Davis. The group included several students from nearby Central High School and Northeast High School, Davis said.
After the birthday party attendees gathered at the park, another group arrived and an argument between the two groups escalated into gunfire, Davis told reporters at a news conference.
All the victims were part of the party, Davis added, saying that he "can't remember the last time we've had this many people shot at one time."
No arrests have been made, and an investigation is ongoing.
The FBI is assisting in the investigation due to the number of people involved, but Davis said all the evidence so far indicates the incident is local.

Published: 16:44 EDT, 27 September 2026 | Updated: 16:45 EDT, 27 September 2026
Taylor Swift continued to fuel anticipation for her Patient Zero music video on Sunday, hours ahead of its premiere at the MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs).
The 36-year-old singer-songwriter used Instagram Stories to upload behind-the-scenes footage discussing her thought process behind the release.
In a short clip recorded on the video set, she reflected, 'Walking through here and seeing the way that [cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki] has lit this and the way the sets are and how brilliantly Ethan [Tobman] has done this production design, I’m kind of rethinking the release of the video.'
She cheekily added, 'Like, I need to figure out a way to get this on TV or something.'
Swift joked in the March 2025 recording, 'I'm like, Ethan, google: when are the VMAs?'
And the songstress wrote along the bottom of the video, 'Turns out the @VMAS are Sept 27 aka today.'
Taylor Swift continued to fuel anticipation for her Patient Zero music video on Sunday, hours ahead of its premiere at the MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs); pictured at the 2024 MTV VMAs
The 36-year-old singer-songwriter used Instagram Stories to upload behind-the-scenes footage discussing her thought process behind the release
Swift, who directed the Patient Zero visual, will receive MTV's inaugural Artist Director Honors at Sunday evening's awards show.
Teasers shared online last week revealed Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell as co-stars in the project.
The song is about a woman who escapes a toxic relationship, then helps guide her ex's current girlfriend, who is also suffering.
'The story behind me writing the song Patient Zero is that I was hanging out with a bunch of friends, and one of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy,' Swift told the UK's Capital FM on Friday.
According to Swift, 'everyone' in the group 'immediately started saying, like, "Oh, I've been through that too," and telling the stories of when this kind of reach-out had happened for them.'
She also said she was thrilled she 'got to explore' the sticky situation in a song.
'I thought to myself, if this has happened to all of us, it's such an interesting kind of angle on humanity and on relationships, and I wonder if I could write something from the perspective of getting this phone call, and really only from the perspective and the side of the phone call of the ex who's been through it before,' she explained.
Swift announced the new single on Tuesday, and on Friday she released the follow-up to last year's The Life of a Showgirl album, titled, The Encore.
The video stars Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell
Johnson (L) and Swift (R) pictured in a still from the impending video
Patient Zero is one of four songs featured on The Life of A Showgirl: The Encore
In addition to Patient Zero, the collection of new music includes the songs Cleveland!, Pink Clouding, and Babylon.
Unfortunately for the Grammy-winning music artist, critics have branded the majority of the tracks 'duds.'
Early reviews panned the tunes, calling them 'derivative and flat.'
However, Swifties are fully embracing her latest output, with Patient Zero crowned Spotify’s most-streamed song by a female artist in a single day this year.
The platform also revealed that Swift has become the most-streamed female artist in a single day in 2026.
Fans can also look forward to the star's forthcoming appearance at the Country Music Awards in November.
Her song I Knew It, I Knew You , from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, is nominated for Single of the Year alongside two Ella Langley songs, as well as tracks by Lainey Wilson and Cody Johnson.
Swift last showed up at the CMAs in 2016, when she presented Garth Brooks with the award for Entertainer of the Year.
This year's event will take place on November 18 at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, hosted by Lainey Wilson.

articles.title_zh: Bomb squad searching vans near U.S. air base in Britain as five men arrested on terror charge
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — British police arrested several men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses on Sunday and evacuated homes near an air base that the U.S. Air Force had been using to facilitate strikes on Iran.
A major incident was declared, with a massive emergency presence seen around RAF Fairford, which is about 90 minutes outside London, close to the village of Whelford in west England.
The Gloucestershire police force said it responded in the early hours of Sunday to reports of three suspicious vehicles moving toward the base, and arrested five men “on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act.” They were later further charged on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
Police did not provide further details on the men, who remain in custody, or what they were suspected to have done. “Work to establish the full nature of this incident is ongoing,” Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said.
Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans of Counter Terrorism Policing said the force is “working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident,” with the investigation still in its “early stages.”
Ocone said 85 homes across the local area were evacuated and a 440-yard cordon put in place while an Army ordnance disposal team examines the vehicles.
Helicopter footage from Sky News showed multiple white vans close to the base seemingly being searched by a bomb disposal robot.
Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, told Britain’s Press Association another resident had reported three suspicious vans in the village. Along with other residents, Tudsbery has since been evacuated to a nearby recreation center.
The Reuters news agency had reported that security measures at the air ‌base have been significantly increased in recent ‌days.
Cotswold District Council member Tristan Wilkinson told NBC News that a threat to the base from Iran about six weeks ago has heightened the alert level in the community and led to a ramped-up police presence and an increase in security patrols.
Wilkinson noted there is “a lot more vigilance from the local community” and that police in this instance “have done exactly what you’d hope they would do in increasing reassurance for the community.”
“This is a worry and escalation, and we wait to see what the nature of that actual incident is going to be,” the official added.
A U.S. European Command spokesperson said: “For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures.”
“U.S. European Command remains vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families across the European theater,” the spokesperson added. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”
Asked about the incident on Sunday after walking off of Air Force One, President Donald Trump told reporters the arrest was an “amazing job.”
“They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great,” he said.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a post on X: “I know today’s incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country.”
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” he added.
“The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts,” Burnham said.
In March this year, Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran.
In July, Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Britain that “any base used to invade Iranian territory is our legitimate target,” Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported, citing bomber aircraft flights from Fairford.
At the time, a British government spokesperson said that the country was “ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad.”
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Raf Sanchez is a foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: White House airs another government-funded ad, this time with Trump warning of ‘final battle’
articles.title_zh: White House airs another government-funded ad, this time with Trump warning of ‘final battle’
articles.content_orig:
John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms
As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump ’s political agenda before the November midterm elections , US senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal.
Kennedy, the US president’s fellow Republican , was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multiple ads featuring Trump – including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign.
Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he had rebuked Kristi Noem , then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a $220m series of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”.
“Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?”
Kennedy replied: “Well, first, as to secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.”
“This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to the first ad in the series , a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists.
“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.”
Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch act , a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities.
According to Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates , the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcast another partisan ad featuring the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday.
That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024.
“This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start a war with Iran that has left some supporters feeling betrayed.
“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem.
after newsletter promotion
The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it was posted on his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters.
The ad was even played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-SPAN on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”.
At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive to put his own name on public buildings.
“I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there is such a statute in his home state.
“Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded, reminding the Republican lawmaker that making statements on Sunday morning television shows is not the same as using his power to actually introduce legislation that could restrain Trump.

articles.content_orig:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sept. 27, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Republican Louisiana Senator John Kennedy. Good morning to you, Senator. Senator, the president seems to be dangling some interest in diplomacy. The U.S. president also seems to be somewhat interested, but the Wall Street Journal is also reporting President Trump has a secret plan to restart the bombing campaign in Iran after the midterm elections. That's 37 days from now. Is that renewed bombing something you support?
SEN. JOHN KENNEDY: Well, I don't know. I haven't seen the classified intelligence. Iran- Iran made an offer recently to the president. It was not a serious offer. The president's not Bambi's baby brother. He turned it down. We need to continue doing what we're doing. The sanctions, the blockade. The truth is, if you- if you're fair minded at all, Iran is a sucking chest wound and the world is safer for it. It's public and private sector is held together with duct tape and spit. Now, there's- there's just one problem. The strait is at least partially closed, and it's affected the price of oil and oil's in everything, including gasoline. And- and it's painful as- as hell. And we've got to either figure out a way to- to settle this thing, to get the strait open or to escalate. I would not send in troops. We could send in troops and we could open the strait. But once you send them in, you've got to leave them there. And that creates a whole new host of problems.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, and the broader question of to what end, since the president has said, you know, Iran is about to capitulate any day now. But when we look at the politics of this out in Iowa and Michigan, we've seen Republican candidates who are going to be on the ballot in November, call for an end to the Iran war. In the Senate, we've seen 14 votes to date, objecting to it- two passed. I mean, I know those are symbolic, but this is reflective of frustration within your own party here. Should the president be more aware of public opinion?
SEN. KENNEDY: Well, look, here's- none of this is advanced calculus. Here's- I've- I've- I've been to just about every battleground state helping my mates. Here's what I've learned. When- when moms and dads lie down to sleep at night and can't, they're not lying there worried about whether the football coaches are happy or whether the press is biased or the other things that we've been talking about. They're worried about the cost of living.
SEN. KENNEDY: And- and they're a little worried about Iran because they don't understand why, but they know the two are inextricably linked. And we've got to be straight up and address those things. Here's my prediction for the midterms, Margaret. The experts will be wrong. They almost always are. Not- not- none of these guys have ever run a campaign in their natural lives. It's going to be close. It would help if the president would stay focused on cost of living. And I would like to see him give a nationwide address.
SEN. KENNEDY: Or let Rubio and General Caine do it and explain why we went into Iran, why we're winning, and how we're going to get out.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. You've been making that recommendation for some time. You did it last time you were with us over the summer. The White House has not to date, but--
SEN. KENNEDY: Well- well- well, the- the- the president doesn't take orders from me. He barely takes suggestions. But I'm pretty persistent, and I'm going to keep recommending it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about something else the executive branch just did without Congress. On Friday, the White House informed Congressional leaders that he, the president, unilaterally canceled nearly $1 billion in Congressionally approved funds and did it without Congress's consent. You sit on Appropriations. The chair of that committee, Susan Collins, said this was the latest attempt to undermine Congress's constitutional power of the purse, and that this is a clear violation of the law. She wants to take action against these illegal actions. Do you share her concern? Are you going to join her effort?
SEN. KENNEDY: I love- I love Susan like a taco, but she's wrong. First, Congress didn't approve this stuff. When Congress appropriates money, we do it in broad care- categories. For example, I'm making this up- $250 million to improve relations with sub-Sahara Africa. And then the money goes to the bureaucracy. And a lot of times the bureaucracy wastes it. Spending porn is what I call it. That's how we ended up with millions of dollars for circumcisions in- in Zambia and electric buses in Rwanda.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you're okay with this?
SEN. KENNEDY: What- what the president- yeah, I'm fine with it. What- what- if you read what- what Russ Vought wants to actually cut, what he wants- what he wants to cut is aid to NGOs who support illegal immigration. And he also wants to cut some money that the bureaucracy has decided to give to help pay down, not our debt, but foreign debt. This stuff- spending porn. Congress didn't approve it. Now Susan is worried about them doing this to the NIH grants. I don't think they ought to do it to the NIH grants, but this is spending porn that they're cutting--
SEN. KENNEDY: --and Congress ought to be- Congress ought to get up off its ice-cold, lazy butt and cut it itself. But since we're not--
SEN. KENNEDY: --I'm glad- I'm glad that Russ Vought's doing it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You're talking about concern about wasteful spending.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You were very sharp in your questioning of then-Secretary Kristi Noem in regard to some ads that DHS had been running, using taxpayer money to bolster her public image. Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program. It's on all major networks, it's on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there's a voice praising him as, quote, "the toughest, most resilient person I ever met." And at the end, it says "paid for by the U.S. government." Is that the best use of taxpayer money?
SEN. KENNEDY: Well, first, as to Secretary Noem, what she did was master class dumb. she spent $220 million on commercials about her, and I called her out on it. Number two--
MARGARET BRENNAN: This looks like a commercial about President Trump.
SEN. KENNEDY: I don't, I- I was just going to say, Margaret, I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on- on private ads for themselves. Now, the White House sees it differently, but I don't- I think there ought to be a rule that you can't- well, there probably is a rule- you can't spend public money to to promote yourself. I'm going to- I may end up with a sombrero on my head, but I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician--
SEN. KENNEDY: --can have a building named after him while he's alive. I think that would settle a lot of this controversy.
SEN. KENNEDY: We have that rule in Louisiana. It works pretty well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we'll watch, Senator, if you introduce that. Thank you for your time this morning. Face the Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Anthropic's Dario Amodei to have White House dinner with Trump
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Anthropic's Dario Amodei to have White House dinner with Trump
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei will join President Donald Trump for a private dinner at the White House on Sunday, CNBC confirmed, in what will be the first one-on-one meeting between the two leaders.
Amodei was noticeably absent from Trump's glitzy state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, as other tech bigwigs — OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg — were photographed rubbing elbows with government officials. Amodei had a scheduling conflict, so Trump invited him to a private dinner, according to a source familiar with the details who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The meeting, first reported by Axios , comes at a high-stakes moment for Anthropic, which is gearing up for what's widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO . The company's precarious relationship with the Trump administration has been under strain for much of the last year, so Amodei's sit-down with the president could serve as a valuable opportunity to ease tensions.
"President Trump has been clear: America will lead the world in Super Intelligence, while protecting American consumers," a White House official said in a statement, in response to CNBC's inquiry about Sunday's dinner. "We will drive innovation, strengthen American competitiveness, and ensure this transformative technology works for the American people."
Amodei drew Trump's ire earlier this month by publicly urging the AI industry to slow down the pace of advanced model development and better address potential risks . He published a three-step proposal and called for additional government oversight, which angered the president even as it gained the support of other industry leaders like Altman and Musk.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social . "The Trump Administration has stopped AI 'people' from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,' like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel' - and we will continue to do so!"
Amodei was already in a difficult spot with the president, because he supported Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election and was a vocal critic of Trump.
But before Amodei's call for a slowdown rocked the tech sector, Anthropic's relationship with the Trump administration appeared to be on the mend.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who temporarily imposed export controls on two of the company's most advanced models in June, told Axios earlier this month that Anthropic is "back on the right side." He also hosted a fireside chat with Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown at the G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina.
Brown, who serves as Anthropic's chief compute officer, has taken on a much more active role in interfacing with the Trump administration in recent months. He reportedly led the company's negotiations with the Commerce Department over its export control directive, replacing Amodei in that role.
"We trust Anthropic," Lutnick said on the sidelines of the event.
That same day, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) Director Michael Kratsios told CNBC that the administration was "in a good cadence" with Anthropic. He said the company was "open" and actively sharing models with the government as part of Trump's voluntary AI executive order.
Anthropic has had less success winning over officials at the Department of Defense, however.
Negotiations between the company and the Pentagon spiraled in February after the two sides failed to agree on how the military could use its models. The DOD wanted Anthropic to grant the military unfettered access to its models across all lawful purposes, while Anthropic wanted assurance that its technology would not be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance.
After talks collapsed, the DOD labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk , an unprecedented move that meant the company purportedly threatened U.S. national security. The designation prevents the U.S. military from using Anthropic's models and blocks defense contractors from using them in their work with the agency.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to reverse it's blacklisting, but the company suffered a blow on Friday after a federal appeals court panel in Washington, D.C., upheld the Pentagon's action . The company could still petition for a rehearing, and could also ask the Supreme Court to take the case.
Emil Michael, the DOD's technology chief, celebrated the ruling in a post on X .
"The hammer of justice has smashed @AnthropicAI arguments," Michael wrote on Friday. "They are a Supply Chain Risk to the defense industrial base serving the @DeptofWar. Warfighters will sleep better knowing that no private company will insert their opinions in the chain of command. @SecWar was right!"
Defense Secretary Hegseth accused Anthropic of "duplicity" and argued that the company attempted "to strong-arm the United States military into submission" when negotiations collapsed in February. He reaffirmed that position in a post on X on Friday.
"Confirmed: @AnthropicAI = Supply Chain Risk," Hegseth wrote. The @DeptofWar does what is right for the Country and our Warriors."

There are a lot of $300-$400 headphones on the market right now, and most of them blur together. I spent the last few weeks with the Sennheiser Momentum 5 to determine if this pair actually stands out, testing everything from sound quality and noise cancellation to comfort and battery life.
At $399.99, the Momentum 5 sit right in the middle of the premium headphone market. That puts them up against the pricier Sony WH-1000XM6 and Apple AirPods Max 2, while offering a more affordable option for anyone looking for high-end headphones.
Starting with sound, vocals sound natural and the bass is strong without taking over. The headphones allow you to start noticing little things in music, like a background harmony or a guitar string that cheaper headphones often tend to miss. If I had to describe the sound in one word, it’d be balanced.
The headphones support Dolby Atmos, which essentially means that music or movies sound like they’re coming from all around you instead of just left and right.
With this generation, Sennheiser doubled the microphone count to eight to improve the active noise cancellation (ANC). Voices and nearby chatter, which are usually the kind of sounds that can cut through weaker ANC, are noticeably quieter. Sennheiser claims this pair is up to three times more effective than the previous generation at blocking this type of noise.
Of course, it’s not quite at the level of blocking out everything like a plane’s engine, but it does the job effectively without making your ears feel weirdly pressurized as can be the case with some ANC headphones.
As for comfort, the headphones aren’t as premium-feeling as Apple or Sony headphones that I’ve tried in the past, but given that the Momentum 5 cost less than its competitors, it’s a trade-off that’s hard to complain about.
The battery life is genuinely impressive. It’s rated for up to 57 hours, and that figure held up in my testing. For context, that’s roughly twice the battery life of the Sony WH-1000XM6 and nearly three times that of the AirPods Max 2.
And when the battery does run out, a 10-minute charge gets you up to seven hours of playback, while a full charge takes about two hours.
A notable difference that the Momentum 5 offers that its competitors don’t is a user-replaceable cell, which means you can swap out the battery once it degrades instead of having to buy a whole new pair.
What I wasn’t expecting, but found surprisingly useful, was how thin the carrying case is. I’ve never really been able to fit a pair of headphones into my medium-sized purses, but the Momentum 5 fit perfectly. It’s also a big plus when traveling, since the case doesn’t take up much space in your luggage.
With the headphones’ companion app, Smart Control Plus, you can adjust a bunch of different settings. There’s an 8-band EQ that lets you tune the sound yourself or choose from one of Sennheiser’s presets. The app also lets you adjust the level of ANC rather than just switching it on or off, and there’s an anti-wind mode you can access there too. The “Sound Personalization” feature walks you through a listening test and creates a sound profile tailored to your hearing preferences.
The app gives you a decent amount of control over the Momentum 5, and I found it pretty easy to navigate as most of the settings are quite straightforward.
Overall, the Sennheiser Momentum 5 is a solid option at this price. They offer great sound, the battery life is excellent, and the downsides are pretty minor. They’re heavier than the Sony WH-1000XM6, and aren’t as comfortable as some Sony or Apple options, but at $399.99, they’re cheaper than both while still delivering where it matters.

articles.title_orig: Report: Apple working on new Vision Pro, with different form factors on the table
articles.title_zh: Report: Apple working on new Vision Pro, with different form factors on the table
articles.content_orig:
After the release of Vision Pro, everyone wanted to know how long it would be before the company could release a lighter version that isn’t so bulky on your face. For the longest time, we had been looking forward to a so-called Vision Air, codenamed N100. That project was shelved last year , though the company is working on a new project with similar aspirations, per Bloomberg .
Unlike the previous N100 project, it doesn’t seem the new project, N224, is necessarily targeted at being a lower cost offering. It could instead be a successor to the current M5-based Vision Pro model, though it might still come in at a lower price while offering the flagship experience.
This new version seems relatively early in the works, with Bloomberg reporting that it could arrive between late 2028 and early 2029. That said, it isn’t quite clear what exactly Apple will be going for. The company currently has four concepts in the works.
One of the concepts is similar to the recently unveiled Meta VR glasses , which offloads the compute and battery to an external puck. Given the fact that Vision Pro already has an external battery, offloading the compute doesn’t necessarily seem like a major hurdle, though you’d need better thermals and more efficient compute to pull that off.
On the other hand, some Apple executives reportedly don’t love the idea of an external puck, and “want the company to stick with something closer to an all-in-one design.”
Design wise, Apple might get a bit more experimental compared to the current Vision Pro, with the company supposedly considering other material choices. From the Power On newsletter :
One design in testing retains the basic egg-shaped form of the current Vision Pro, but Apple is actively exploring ways to reduce its weight by experimenting with plastic, titanium, other metals and various materials. The company has also continued to explore a standalone puck that combines the computing components and battery, similar to the approach used by Meta’s recent VR Glasses.
Time will tell what Apple will actually end up delivering. Given the A20 Pro chip being incredibly performant at its thermal envelope, it seems highly likely that in another 2 years, we could have an A-series chip capable of running visionOS at a higher capacity than the current M5, while not needing active cooling.
I do think Apple should go all in on the Meta VR glasses idea. Even at a higher price point, I think the form factor makes a ton of sense. Apple silicon, EyeSight, and visionOS will allow the product stand out.

articles.title_orig: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks encampment protest in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.title_zh: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks encampment protest in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Supporters had gathered outside her building overnight on Friday, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.
The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to fierce public anger.
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction, some setting off flares. They carried placards reading “Not one more eviction, not one less neighbor, we are all Maricarmen” and “right to housing at a fair price.”
At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza, some pitching tents. They remained in place early Sunday as dozens of activists staged a sit-in. A model of a vulture, decrying so-called “vulture funds,” hung above the camp.
Earlier in the week, tenants unions and other housing groups held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza.
An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.
Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.
“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”
Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.
“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.
Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.
The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.
The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.
Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.
“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”
Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.
“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”
Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.
“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.
It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with  politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”
“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”
Jamie Gray is a senior desk editor for NBC News based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
articles.title_zh: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
articles.content_orig:
Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.
Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.
In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks.
In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.
Police said thirteen men and four women were killed.
Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African.
He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups.
Mining without permission in abandoned shafts or dump sites is a persistent problem in South Africa, causing numerous deaths from unsafe conditions. Authorities say the miners are typically undocumented migrants recruited by organised crime gangs.
Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP.
He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.
In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.
No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.
The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.
Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million.
But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence.
On Saturday, a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni , to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths.

articles.title_orig: Swiss say no to hardening neutrality principle, safeguarding sanctions on Russia
articles.title_zh: Swiss say no to hardening neutrality principle, safeguarding sanctions on Russia
articles.content_orig:
Swiss voters appear to have rejected a proposal to introduce a more rigid enforcement of the country's neutrality principle — repudiating an idea which would have made imposing sanctions against Moscow more difficult.
In a referendum which took place Sunday, around 7 out of 10 Swiss participants  voted against the "safeguard Swiss neutrality" initiative, according to projections from the Swiss polling institute GFS Bern. Early official results put the "no" camp at 68%, with a participation rate of 46%. Counting is still in progress.
If the proposal had been approved, Switzerland's neutrality, enshrined in the Constitution since 1848, would have been interpreted more strictly, with the country not joining or participating in any military or security alliance, and not imposing sanctions on hostile states.
There were concerns that a “yes” vote would have effectively prevented Switzerland from imposing sanctions on Russia — unless they were approved by the United Nations Security Council, where Moscow has veto power.
Russia openly backed the initiative, which was introduced by the right-wing Pro Switzerland organization. Pro Swizerland argued that Swiss neutrality should always be applied and "not adjusted on a case-by-case or ad hoc basis."
Switzerland has largely mirrored the EU's sanctions against Moscow. The country expanded its sanctions list in mid-August, following the EU's 20th sanctions package.
Both the Swiss government and the Swiss Parliament had advised rejecting the proposal. Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis, who leads the country's foreign affairs department, had said that the country's current neutrality regime "has proved its worth."
Swiss voters face another neutrality question later this year. In November, they will be asked to assess whether Switzerland's arms export rules are still fit for purpose or whether the country should be allowed to export weapons to a defined group of 25 mostly Western countries, even if they are involved in an ongoing conflict.
If approved, that change would tighten Swiss ties with Western countries and could boost its defense industry's export earnings.

WASHINGTON — Since the 2024 election, Democratic congressional candidates have reached a consensus about how to broadly discuss the border — make it secure — but they still lack a cohesive message about ICE.
Some advocate abolishing the agency, while others offer visions for how to rein it in and reform it.
Meanwhile, for Republicans, President Trump’s immigration policies have offered a win on one issue (the border) while creating another issue  that many voters find troubling (violence during raids).
Some battleground Republicans are distancing themselves from Trump and have shifted from talking about mass deportations to emphasizing deporting criminals.
Most voters don’t care more about immigration than the cost of living. But it remains an important issue, and for both Republicans and Democrats, the balance in messaging about immigration is delicate, as about half of Americans see the administration’s tactics against immigrants as too aggressive.
As the Nov. 3 midterms approach, Democratic candidates in various states including Illinois, Minnesota and New Jersey have said Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished. In Michigan, progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has said as much — and taken aim at fellow party members.
“The idea that somehow we can’t say ‘abolish ICE’ because we’re so afraid of what they’re going to say, when we’ve seen ICE terrorize people in our streets,” he said before Michigan’s Senate primary in July. “To me, it is exactly the kind of cowardice that we don’t need from Democrats.”
The Democratic dilemma was crystallized last month when Democratic National Committee members approved dueling messages — one to abolish ICE, the other to reform it.
Among those in the reform camp is Randy Villegas, the political science professor running against Rep. David Valadao (R-Hanford) in California’s Central Valley.
Villegas is in favor of a pathway to citizenship for longtime immigrants as well as a secure border. He’s called for ending the use of for-profit detention facilities and prosecuting ICE agents who engage in illegal conduct.
It’s a personal issue too. Villegas is the son of immigrants from Mexico, and, according to a 2021 NPR story, his brother is a DACA recipient , granted protection under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. He said the constituents of the mostly rural 22nd District deserve a representative who understands the effects of the broken immigration system; he recalls his mother being unable to visit her sister when she was dying of cancer.
“Kern County was ground zero for these ICE raids last year. What did Valadao do or say about it? Absolutely nothing. This is somebody who likes to pretend they’re a moderate on immigration. He voted to triple ICE’s budget,” Villegas said in an interview, noting that he organized a local workshop with immigration attorneys.
After the raids, led by Customs and Border Protection agents who were reported to have gone “rogue” weeks before President Biden left office, Valadao released a statement saying he had spoken to agency officials and urged them to target “criminals rather than those responsible for producing our nation’s food supply.”
The 22nd District is one of fewer than two dozen toss-up races nationwide that will likely determine which party controls the U.S. House in the second half of President Trump’s term.
Valadao , a dairy farmer and the son of immigrants from the Azores islands of Portugal, says on his campaign website that he supports a “reasonable and responsible” pathway to citizenship, a guest worker program that could stabilize the agricultural workforce and a focus on removing immigrants who have committed serious crimes.
Last year, he sponsored the Dignity Act , a bipartisan bill that would create a new temporary legal status for immigrants who meet certain requirements and pass a criminal background check.
Valadao declined an interview request but said in a statement that “our immigration system is broken after decades of inaction, and it’s critical that we restore law and order while recognizing the contributions of people who have lived and worked peacefully in our communities for years.”
In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico frequently has said that the southern border should be treated “like our front porch,” with a welcome mat and a lock on the door.
Talarico says immigration enforcement is necessary but that resources should be refocused to target cartels, gang members and human traffickers. As for ICE, he said the government should “tear down this secret police force and replace it with an agency that is actually going to focus on public safety.”
Centrist Democratic strategists said Talarico’s messaging strikes the right tone for swing voters.
During the Biden administration, voters lost trust with Democrats on immigration and border security, said Sarah Pierce, a former U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services official who leads immigration work at the center-left think tank Third Way. That needs to stay top of mind for Democratic candidates, she said.
“Americans don’t trust that Democrats are even willing to enforce immigration laws, so obviously there’s a lot of pressure on the party to rectify that,” Pierce said. “At the same time, this is the most anti-immigrant administration we’ve had in history.”
Talarico’s opponent, Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton, touts Trump’s hard-line immigration policies and has made border security a key part of his campaign.
Paxton also believes states should work with the federal government on immigration enforcement. This year, his office conducted raids in Houston and transferred 50 immigrants to ICE custody.
Matt Terrill, a Republican strategist who was chief of staff for then-Sen. Marco Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign, said Republican candidates need Trump to turn out the GOP base so they retain control of Congress.
Some Republican candidates are conveying a more nuanced message, but it might not matter to voters who already feel betrayed by Trump. That’s the assessment of Matthew Dallek, a political historian at George Washington University who studies Republican and Homeland Security politics.
“A lot of Republican candidates are struggling to figure out a message on what had been a great political strength that has turned into a major liability,” Dallek said. “Different Republicans are giving different answers to try to appeal to the Latino vote, maybe to independents, to voters who might typically vote Republican and support closed borders, but think that ICE has gone too far.”
Many Republican candidates aren’t avoiding immigration. A Third Way analysis of last month’s spending on immigration-related ads in competitive House and Senate races found that Republicans had spent more than $50 million — five times more than Democrats.
At issue, however, is the messaging. Earlier this year, White House officials and House Republican leaders reportedly told their members to avoid talking about “mass deportations” and talk up removing criminals.
The potential changes, announced Wednesday, would exclude undocumented immigrants, asylum seekers and anyone without permanent status. Certain demographic questions from the traditional questionnaire would also be eliminated.
Rep. Gabe Evans , who is running for reelection in Colorado, described the distinction as “gangbangers, not grandmas.”
At the Republican National Convention in 2024, Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas) denounced “open borders” before a crowd waving signs reading “mass deportation now!”
As the Trump administration’s enforcement campaign took shape, however, she signed a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson calling on ICE to focus its resources on arresting immigrants with criminal records, and in March she intervened after local high school mariachi performers

articles.title_orig: CFB Overtime: Florida's Jon Sumrall is making every right move, coaching pressure mounts, top Week 4 takeaways
articles.title_zh: CFB Overtime: Florida's Jon Sumrall is making every right move, coaching pressure mounts, top Week 4 takeaways
articles.content_orig:
Welcome back, Florida Gators.
We’ve missed you more than you know.
We’ve missed the noise, the swagger, the arrogance, the audacity. We’ve missed the big games in a bonkers Swamp when 90,000 fans show up expecting something spectacular instead of bracing for something stupid. Most of all, college football has missed the mighty Gators being the mighty Gators.
On a sunny, honey of a Saturday afternoon, No. 21 Florida didn’t merely beat No. 4 Ole Miss. The Gators bludgeoned the Rebels 52-28 , snapped a 12-game losing streak against Top 5 opponents and sent a message reverberating from Gainesville to every corner of the SEC: The Gators are back. Back among the relevant. Back among the dangerous. Back among the elite.
A week ago, college football was buzzing about Lane Kiffin returning to Oxford to play the program he left high and dry. This week, it’s about the coach Florida hired instead of Kiffin beating the ever-loving Hotty Toddy out of Ole Miss.
“This has very little to do with me,” Sumrall said during his on-field interview afterward.
It has everything to do with him.
That’s all it has taken Sumrall to pump more electricity into Florida football than the previous four head coaches could generate with jumper cables and a lightning bolt. Earlier this week, when told the Gators were actually favored over No. 4 Ole Miss by oddsmakers in Las Vegas, Sumrall cracked, “There are a lot of good drugs out there, huh.”
Turns out there is one particularly powerful drug going around Gainesville these days. It’s called belief, and Sumrall has injected it straight into the veins of Gator Nation.
Yes, there were brief bursts of excitement under Will Muschamp, Jim McElwain and Dan Mullen. But none of them – and certainly not Billy Napier – created this immediate jolt of energy, personality and possibility. The excitement around Florida football isn’t merely palpable; it’s intoxicating.
And nothing demonstrates the difference between Sumrall and Napier more than the offense. Napier stubbornly tried to do everything himself. He surrounded himself with familiar faces and produced an offense that looked like it needed an instruction manual to figure out but was almost always as dull as a butter knife.
One of Sumrall’s first moves? He went out and hired offensive coordinator Buster Faulkner from Georgia Tech and gave him a $2.1 million annual salary – more than any assistant coach in UF history.
What a concept: Hire really good coaches and let them coach.
Florida entered Saturday with the nation’s No. 3 offense after finishing 104th last season. Then the Gators hung 52 on the No. 4 team in America – the most points Florida has scored against a Top 5 opponent since Steve Spurrier’s Gators annihilated Florida State 52-20 in the 1997 Sugar Bowl to win the national championship.
Gator fans, enjoy Faulkner while you can. If this continues, he’ll be a head coach next season. Maybe even in Tallahassee.
That would be appropriate because this offense is starting to look like something out of Florida’s glorious past. With just over four minutes remaining and Florida leading 45-28, the Gators could have run out the clock, shaken hands and called it a day.
They threw deep to Eric Singleton Jr., setting up another touchdown and putting 52 on the scoreboard. It was positively Spurrierian. Why kneel when you can score? Why survive when you can humiliate? Why just win when you can make the scoreboard scream?
And nobody is making more noise than Jadan Baugh. The signs in the Swamp said it all: “In Awe of Baugh.” “Run the Damn Baugh.” And the description that seems more appropriate with every passing week: He is Bad to the Baugh.
Baugh carried 29 times for 142 yards and three touchdowns, giving him five consecutive 100-yard games. The only other Gators ever to do that? Emmitt Smith and Fred Taylor.
That’s not a list. That’s a shrine.
Baugh also has multiple rushing touchdowns in five straight games, the longest such SEC streak since Derrick Henry’s Heisman season at Alabama in 2015. And, yes, Baugh was scoring touchdowns and striking the Heisman pose.
Before the game, Florida legend Tim Tebow told the cheering “SEC Nation” crowd in Gainesville: “Some people do the Heisman pose out of hope. I love Jadan because he does it out of belief.”
Believe it now: Jadan Baugh is a legitimate Heisman Trophy candidate.
And here’s the scary part: When Baugh needed a breather, Duke Clark came in and ran for 126 yards himself, including a 45-yard touchdown in which he juked Ole Miss defenders into another ZIP code. Together, Baugh and Clark helped Florida pile up 302 rushing yards and six touchdowns on the ground.
This wasn’t finesse. This was a mugging.
For years, Florida fans kept hearing about rebuilds and patience and culture and process. Enough process. Give them progress. Give them points. Give them victories. Give them Saturdays when the Swamp shakes again.
Sumrall spent the offseason calling Florida a “sleeping giant” and talking about “waking the beast.”
Consider the alarm clock smashed.
Said Sumrall of that sleeping giant: “It’s not asleep, but it ain’t fully awake yet. It’s being stirred up a little bit. We’re going to get there. It’s coming. I didn’t come here for us to be average. We had some recruits here this weekend. We get a lot of those guys to say yes, and we’re going to wake up the beast real fast.”
Florida is 4-0 for the first time since 2019. The Gators have scored at least 50 points three times in four games, only the second time in school history that’s been accomplished. On Saturday, they scored touchdowns on five consecutive second-half possessions against the No. 4 team in America.
Maybe there will be bumps ahead. There always are in the SEC. They still have the No. 1 and No. 2 teams in America – Texas and Georgia – on their schedule. But this feels different, looks different and sounds different. The Swamp is roaring again. The offense is rolling again. A Heisman candidate is posing again. And, perhaps most importantly, Florida football is swaggering again.
For too many years, the Gators kept telling us they were on their way back. On Saturday, they quit sending postcards and finally arrived.
College football hasn’t been the same without you.

Four American tourists were among six people killed in Greece when a devastating explosion leveled a residential building near Athens’ famed Acropolis, according to officials.
The four Americans — two men and two women believed to be two couples — were staying in the two-story building in the historic Plaka district, the historic neighborhood at the foot of the Acropolis and close to some of Athens’ most heavily visited landmarks, when the blast struck Friday.
The two couples had been expected to catch a flight from Athens airport at 3 p.m. Friday but never showed up, a police source told Reuters. Documents and belongings recovered with the four victims indicated they were U.S. citizens, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media.
AMERICAN TOURISTS STABBED OUTSIDE ATHENS' ACROPOLIS AS POLICE DETAIN SUSPECT IN APPARENT RANDOM ATTACK
Firefighters work at the scene following Friday's powerful blast in Athens' Plaka district, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis)
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle mourned the victims in a post on X.
"I am deeply saddened to learn of the death of four American citizens in yesterday’s explosion in central Athens," Guilfoyle wrote.
Emergency crews searching through the rubble recovered six bodies from the collapsed building Saturday, authorities said.
Firefighters had been searching for an elderly couple who lived in one apartment and four tourists staying in another as crews painstakingly removed debris, fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis said in a televised briefing.
EXPLOSION NEAR GERMAN TRAIN STATION INJURES 2 UKRAINIAN CITIZENS
The explosion was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Authorities were investigating the cause after reports of a gas smell in the area.
Firefighters work at the scene following Friday's powerful blast in Athens' Plaka district, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis)
The powerful blast destroyed the building and damaged nearby homes, shops and vehicles, sending rubble and shattered glass as far as three blocks away, Reuters reported.
Video from the scene showed debris strewn across the street and parked cars crushed beneath falling rubble. The destroyed building was reduced to twisted metal, broken tiles and concrete, with clothing and household belongings scattered among the wreckage.
Rescuers work at the scene following Friday's powerful blast in Athens' Plaka district, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis)
The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, while crews also used cameras and sensors to comb through the debris.
Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, according to the fire department. Resident Andreas Martzaklis told the Associated Press that all those rescued from the neighboring building were tourists.

The UFC has issued a statement on the health condition of veteran bantamweight fighter Raoni Barcelos following UFC Vegas 121.
Here is the UFC’s statement in full, which was issued several hours after the conclusion of UFC Vegas 121 :
“Following his fight tonight, Raoni Barcelos was immediately transported to a Level 1 trauma center for evaluation. The hospital medical team conducted a CT scan and comprehensive assessment, and he is currently being monitored. Barcelos is stable, alert and responsive, with full movement. He will remain under medical supervision. We will provide updates on his condition as they become available,” the UFC said in a statement posted on its official website .
Barcelos was up on the scorecards in the main event of UFC Vegas 121 against Raul Rosas Jr., but ended up losing via fifth-round TKO when he suffered some sort of medical emergency in what can only be described as a scary situation .
At first, it appeared that Barcelos may have been knocked out from a takedown, but it soon became clear that something else was happening as he did not appear to be moving, and with the situation being as concerning as it was, he was immediately rushed to a local Las Vegas hospital.
Fans online were understandably frightened by what was playing out on their screen, as it was one of the scariest situations we have ever seen in a UFC fight. Fortunately, it appears that Barcelos is going to be okay .
While Barcelos’s health is obviously of the utmost concern, it is worth mentioning that he put on an absolutely incredible performance against Rosas, as both fighters won $100,000 in bonuses for Fight of the Night.
It is truly unfortunate for Barcelos that he was just a few minutes away from winning his sixth straight fight and picking up arguably the biggest win of his UFC career to date before he suffered the medical emergency.
However, despite the defeat, it was an amazing performance, and one he should be proud to look back on once he gets fully healthy.

articles.title_zh: The deeper reason behind the relentless rise in bond yields
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Over the past few days, you have probably been hit over the head with stories about rising bond yields.
I hate to admit it, but I even churned out a host of stories on yields this week. Love me a good headline!
The rise in yields is one of the most important things happening in markets right now. Actually, this started in the summer, but you know what I mean.
"I would say [it's] not a crisis but an eye-opener, and it's something I think you've got to think about," BlackRock chief investment officer of global fixed income Rick Rieder said on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed .
Rieder was among the finalists for the Fed chair role that ended up going to Kevin Warsh.
But I don't want you to lose focus on the "why" behind the move. It's not because of some warning on the nation's debt from some third-rate investing pundit. That's not the reason at all.
The reason is that the economy is weakening under the tightening grip of inflation. And this is going down just as the Federal Reserve makes it costlier for businesses and you, the consumer, to borrow money.
Here are a few red flags I have picked up on this week that no one is talking about, other than me.
Execs at payroll services company Paychex ( PAYX ) said this week that we are in a low-hire, low-fire environment. Hardly a bullish economic endorsement.
Lucky Charms maker General Mills ( GIS ) warned about more quarters of pressured margins at the hands of a big pickup in inflation in things like wheat, diesel, and packaging. I think this sheds light on what the Fed hawks like New York Fed president John Williams are telling us about rate hikes.
Cracker Barrel ( CBRL ) called out a 6.1% traffic drop in its most recent quarter. Darden ( DRI ) said sales at its Olive Garden chain grew just 1.1% in the quarter. The read: Much higher gas prices are swallowing up the disposable income of many households.
It's always important to know the "why" when it comes to markets — and sadly, the "why" isn't great in the case of yields.

articles.title_orig: Ruby on Rails Creator Declares 'Pencils Down' on Handwritten Code
articles.title_zh: Ruby on Rails Creator Declares 'Pencils Down' on Handwritten Code
articles.content_orig:
A coding legend is waving goodbye to handwritten code.
David Heinemeier Hansson — commonly known as DHH — is the creator of the popular webapp framework Ruby on Rails. He also runs the software company 37signals, where he just instituted a new rule: "We're done writing code by hand."
"We are going, and have gone, pencils down," Hansson said during the Rails World keynote.
At his software company, 37signals, Hansson said that hand-writing code was an "exceptional state," only to be performed when something went wrong with the AI-generated code.
When an AI agent isn't able to produce what the engineers want, they can "get the old pencil out and dot it down for them," Hansson said — but then they "fix the machine."
"This is a recognition of what is already happening," he said.
Indeed, coding has radically transformed in the last year, thanks to AI tools like OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's Claude Code, and Cursor.
Some developers call coding agents exhilarating, and they stay up late into the night to build with them. Others call AI coding a lonely or tiresome process .
What do engineers actually think? Business Insider polled over 150 software engineers in January about the rise of vibe coding. Over 45% of respondents said they felt they were "keeping up" with AI tools. 17.5% of respondents said they were opting out of using AI code-editing tools entirely.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
There's only one "serious question" in this moment of coding, Hansson said at the keynote: how to best reap the rewards of AI. "Every other question is below that in the stack of values," he said.
Hansson surveyed the audience: "How many people here are still writing material amounts of code by hand on a weekly basis?"
After watching the crowd, Hansson let out an expletive. "That's about five," he said.
