articles.title_orig: China teen blows away the field for record-setting gold at 'sad' Games
articles.title_zh: China teen blows away the field for record-setting gold at 'sad' Games
articles.content_orig:
China's 18-year-old Yan Ziyi showcased her rare talent by shattering the Asian Games record to win the javelin, as a medallist failed a doping test and a decorated badminton player branded the event in Japan "sad".
Golds were up for grabs on day eight in sports including athletics, diving, skateboarding, squash and weightlifting.
On another wet day in Aichi-Nagoya, the teenager Yan demolished the opposition in the women's javelin with her first and only throw of the night of 70.46m.
It was a new Games record, smashing the 66.09m by compatriot Liu Shiying in 2018, and left Japan's reigning Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi in a distant second for silver (62.70m).
Yan's incredible throw was the sixth best of all time. The world record is 72.28m by Barbora Spotakova in 2008.
But Yan is closing in -- she hurled 71.74m in May, the second best of all time.
On the track, Thailand's Puripol Boonson made it a sprint double, winning the men's 200m to go with his 100m crown.
His scintillating 19.88sec equalled the Asian record.
Asked how much faster he can run, the 20-year-old said: "I can't say how fast it's going to be, but it's going to be more records and faster."
Towards the end of day eight, China topped the medals table with 119 golds, with Japan second on 37 and South Korea on 20.
North Korea enjoyed more record-setting success in weightlifting, taking their overall haul in the sport to six golds out of an available 10 so far.
China maintained their unbeaten start in diving, while a pair of teenagers took gold in the street skateboarding finals.
China's Zhu Yuanling, 15, won the women's event and the 17-year-old Juni Kang of South Korea took the men's title.
Kang now has his eyes on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"I want to be No.1 in LA," he said.
Malaysia reigned in the squash, with Ng Eain Yow winning the men's crown and compatriot Sivasangari Subramaniam prevailing in the women's singles.
Both booked spots to Los Angeles in the process.
Organisers in Aichi-Nagoya did not build a traditional athletes' village in a bid to save money, with competitors instead staying in hotels or temporary wooden units, and on a cruise ship.
India's multiple badminton medallist H.S. Prannoy said that made for a disappointing experience.
"It was sad," the 34-year-old, who won team bronze, said in a YouTube video published by the Badminton Association of India.
"It never felt like we were playing in an Asian Games, to be honest."
There have been a series of problems at the Games, including a shortage of rooms, long delays at the airport and poor transport services.
Uzbekistan's Nodirbek Shavkatov became the first medallist at the Games to test positive for doping.
Shavkatov, who won bronze in mixed martial arts, has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium, the International Testing Agency said.
The drug is a prescription heart medication that can improve endurance and accelerates muscle recovery.

articles.title_orig: Meta’s VR Glasses Are What the Apple Vision Pro Should Have Been
articles.title_zh: Meta’s VR Glasses Are What the Apple Vision Pro Should Have Been
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is continuing his metaverse while simultaneously pushing forward on AI agents.
At Meta Connect , the Facebook co-founder revealed on Wednesday the Meta VR Glasses, a smaller and slimmer device compared to the company's older Quest-branded family of VR headsets, and a handheld device called the Muse Charm that works with the company's recently released Muse AI personal agent . He revealed the products while speaking on stage at the annual Connect conference for developers.
Zuckerberg shared few details about what Muse Charm can do, only to say that people will be able to speak to the gadget to interact with their Meta AI agents "without having to unlock a phone or open an app." He didn't say how much it would cost, but said that Meta needs to "finalize laying out the components" and is "planning to have this ready to ship in time for the holidays in December."
"We've packed a lot of technology with this little guy," Zuckerberg said. "So, if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The Meta VR Glasses are slimmer and lighter than the company's older Quest-branded VR headsets, but they are also more expensive, costing $1,299 when they go on sale in spring 2027. They represent Meta's first VR device since 2024, when the company debuted the $299 Quest 3S. The Meta VR Glasses are powered by an external puck that houses a Qualcomm processor and battery, allowing it to function as a mini-computer that also helps reduce the glasses' overall weight and size. The glasses are able to display better visuals than the older Quest headset, and contain sensors that track users' eyes and hand movements, which reduces the need to use controllers to interact with the device.
"We have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion, high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time," Zuckerberg said.

articles.title_orig: Sen. John Fetterman says it's "entirely possible" Democrats take back Senate, says "let's revisit after the midterm" on his plans
articles.title_zh: Sen. John Fetterman says it's "entirely possible" Democrats take back Senate, says "let's revisit after the midterm" on his plans
articles.content_orig:
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said Saturday that it's "entirely possible" his party could win control of the Senate in the midterm elections, but he also left the door open on his own political future.
"Let's revisit after the midterm," Fetterman told CBS News' Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin .
Democrats faced an uphill battle heading into the midterm cycle as they sought control the upper chamber, with 53 Republicans currently in the Senate and a map that appeared more favorable to the GOP. But as affordability issues have persisted in the Trump administration and amid the unpopular war with Iran, the picture has appeared to improve for Democrats as they aim to secure a majority in the Senate.
Fetterman, who delivered Democrats a crucial victory in a closely watched race in 2022, has been under scrutiny in recent years for breaking with his party, spurring questions about his future. Asked whether he would leave the Democratic Party, Fetterman said Saturday that he doesn't "have a reason to." And he emphasized, "I am not a Republican." But he cautioned that people should wait until the midterm elections to "see what I do."
"Let's see what happens if I happen to be 51 — I don't know," Fetterman said.
Fetterman shocked many Democrats when he made a video appearance at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month introducing his counterpart, GOP Sen. Dave McCormick, while vowing to work with President Trump on steel.
But Fetterman said Saturday, "I have no path as a Republican."
The Pennsylvania Democrat said, "There are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party."
"How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterm and see what happens," he said. "And now, if we do win and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania."
Pennsylvania is one of only two states in the country represented by one Democrat and one Republican in the Senate, alongside Wisconsin. A third state, Maine, has one Republican senator and one independent who caucuses with Democrat. Pennsylvania has flipped between supporting Democrats and Republican presidents in recent elections.
On whether he'll seek reelection in 2028 , Fetterman said he's been actively fundraising, but he also indicated that the decision will come after the midterms.
Fetterman posed the question, "Where's the Democratic Party at right now?" He pointed to attendance at a nearby event with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and "the energy" among the party, which has seen a series of wins by insurgent Democrats in recent months. He cited his commitment to Israel as an issue underscoring his divergence from some of the party, adding, "more and more members of my caucus are becoming more and more anti-Israel."
He also pointed to the recent government shutdowns as an issue he diverged from the bulk of Democrats on, arguing that he's "putting the country over the party" and fighting for workers.
"Do you think it's right and smart to shut our government down? No, Democrats, we used to say, 'No, never, never do that,'" Fetterman said. "And that put me at the odds of my caucus, saying, 'It's wrong.'"
Fetterman said he's "chosen to be country over the party, knowing that some of these decisions are going to put me at odds."
Asked whether he expects Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to remain leader if Democrats take the majority, and whether he would vote for him, Fetterman said, "Yes, I mean, there's no one making a move."
Fetterman called a Marist poll that shows Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek up eight points in Iowa "shocking," among other races where Democrats are leading in some polls. He pointed to Schumer's recruiting efforts, saying, "If people are angry at Chuck Schumer, it's undeniable, he has recruited an incredibly strong class."
"I don't sharpen blades for Chuck Schumer, and there might be some people there that refuse to say it, but it's not helpful to go after our leader because we have no idea until we wait until the midterm," Fetterman said. "It's irrelevant until what happens in the midterm."

There’s no way to sugarcoat it. Injuries have sucked a lot of air out of the balloon that is the young season.
That’s not just from a fantasy perspective; every football fan wants to watch Caleb Williams , Jayden Daniels , Brock Bowers and Puka Nacua on Sundays. The sport is better when those guys are playing.
But in fantasy, we strategically picked guys like Nico Collins , Saquon Barkley and DJ Moore to help us win our leagues. Now we have to hear the friend who autodrafted boast about being 2-0? Not ideal.
This makes finding sneaky values that much more important. Not every addition has to be a league-winner -- my goal right now is to get you those week-winning stopgaps while your stars are on the mend.
With that being said, welcome to the infirmary of Week 3.

I did not expect to include Smith here at any point this season. But, as so often happens when we write him off, he doesn’t write back . The Lions have given up the most completions (55), second-most passing yards (658) and second-most passing touchdowns (six) through two weeks. I’m expecting a massive day out of Stroud regardless of who suits up at receiver for Houston.
I told myself I wouldn’t be going near any more Titans this season. But I’ve also told myself that I wouldn’t go near the ice cream aisle at the grocery store. We all know how that story ends. This matchup is that circumstance. Pollard leads all RBs (min. 12 carries) with a 66.7% rush yards over expected rate in 2026, while his 4.7 yards per carry and 1.1 yards over expected per carry each rank in the top 14. Meanwhile, the Giants have allowed the most rush yards over expected per carry (1.7) and highest rate of rushes over expected (57.9%) to running backs this season. I don’t know about you, but I can taste the chocolate ice cream, marshmallows and almonds already.
I laid out the Colts’ defensive deficiencies versus the pass earlier, but I assure you, the run defense ain’t much better . Yes, they played against Derrick Henry and Kenneth Walker III in the first two weeks, but Indianapolis has given up the second-most fantasy points to RBs this season (68.4). The Colts have allowed 1,029 total yards in two games, for crying out loud.

Marks’ PPR upside is high, and if he finds the end zone for the first time since Week 14 of last season, we all go home happy.

His 2.8 yards per route leads all Eagles wide receivers and ranks seventh among WRs with at least 50 routes this season. His 14.7 yards per target leads all wide receivers with at least 10 targets.
More than anything, Wicks has been a big-play weapon with four explosive plays (20+ yards) this season. On Monday night, he will face a Bears defense allowing the league’s fourth-highest explosive pass rate (22.4%). Wicks should be heavily involved in the offense, especially if Saquon Barkley can’t go due to his stinger injury.
Speaking of big-play threats, Thornton might be the boom-or-bust play of the week. After putting up a goose egg in the opener, he had a solid outing last week, catching all four of his targets for 86 yards, including the third-longest grab of his career on a 45-yard deep ball that traveled a whopping 43 air yards. That’s kind of his thing -- Thornton’s 22.8 air yards per target is the highest among WRs with at least 30 routes this season.
Then there’s the Dolphins’ pass defense, which is allowing a league-high 0.5 EPA per dropback and +9.3% completion percentage over expected. The deep ball is squarely in play, considering Miami’s 70.6% success rate allowed on downfield (10+ air yards) pass attempts is third-highest in football. All it takes is one deep touchdown pass to Thornton to potentially win your matchup this week. Why not let it fly?
Is it true that Barner has fewer catches than Noah Fant , fewer yards than Tommy Tremble and hasn’t caught a touchdown pass in the regular season since Week 17 of last year? Yes, it is. But I think that all changes this week, and he doesn’t even need to catch the ball to have fantasy upside.
Barner’s going up against a Washington defense that has given up the third-most fantasy points to TEs this season (44.0), with each starter the Commanders have faced in 2026 ( Dallas Goedert and Jake Ferguson ) scoring two touchdowns against them. Then there’s the second part, which is "The Barnyard" -- Seattle’s version of "The Tush Push," where Barner’s tush is the one being pushed. He scored on that play in Washington last year, and did the same last week against Arizona. If it’s not one, it’ll be the other on Sunday.
Just like in 2025, it appears that all tight ends are viable in fantasy when going up against Cincinnati. Last season, the Bengals allowed the most completions (116), yards (1,444) and touchdowns (16) to the position; as such, they surrendered 357 fantasy points to TEs, the most in the league by a healthy amount. So far in 2026, they again lead the league in yards allowed to tight ends (200).
This is all great news for Freiermuth, who is quietly the TE11 this season and the only Steelers offensive player to find paydirt in 2026. Oh, and you’ll never guess who he has the most catches, yards and touchdowns against -- by comfortable margins, I might add -- in his career. I’ll give you a hint: It rhymes with angles!
This is less about the prowess of Jacksonville’s defense and more about the Patriots’ propensity to put the pill in the palms of the opposition. New England’s five giveaways are tied for the second-most in the NFL -- four of them have been interceptions thrown by Drake Maye , all on his signature deep ball. Only Cooper Rush can say he’s thrown that many picks, and we might not see Rush play again this year.
Seattle was tied for the third-highest scoring D/ST performance against the Pats in Week 1 and then the Steelers were a top-10 unit in Foxborough in Week 2 . Until I see Maye and company figure things out -- which I’m not expecting while A.J. Brown is out -- I’ll happily stream whoever plays them.

A pair of giant pandas departed from Chengdu in south-west China early on Sunday morning, travelling to their new home in Atlanta under a joint agreement between the Chinese and American governments.
While attending a three-day summit in Washington with US president Donald Trump , Chinese president Xi Jinping stated that the bears would arrive in Atlanta over the coming days.
The temporary transfer of the pandas to the zoo was among the few concrete outcomes to emerge from the state visit, which produced public displays of goodwill between the leaders but failed to settle long-standing diplomatic differences between the two nations.
Atlanta said goodbye to its final pandas in 2024, leaving its zoo without any of the animals. A fresh arrangement was initially announced back in April, though specific dates were not released.
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the adult pandas assigned to Zoo Atlanta for a period of 10 years as part of the deal. Both animals were born in 2020 and cared for at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. Ping Ping, a male, possesses distinct dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, a female, features a slightly protruding forehead, according to the Xinhua News Agency.
Beijing has long employed pandas as instruments of global diplomacy, loaning the bears as a sign of goodwill while allowing contracts to lapse when international relations become strained.
Xi described the loan programme as a demonstration of "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."
Earlier this week, Trump met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time, with talks taking place on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
In a largely warm shared press conference, the president praised Burnham as a “natural business person” and the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he had “established a good connection” with Trump.
The prime minister said that the pair had “taken that further today” as they discussed trade, energy and immigration among other topics during their 40-minute meeting.
Trump told reporters: “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”

articles.title_orig: South Africa reels from spate of mass shootings that killed 38 people in a week
articles.title_zh: South Africa reels from spate of mass shootings that killed 38 people in a week
articles.content_orig:
A police officer is seen at a scene of a mass shooting at a house party in KwaMakhutha township south of the city Durban, South Africa, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. STR/AP hide caption
Johannesburg — A spate of mass shootings in three major South African cities killed nearly 40 people this week, with such incidents increasingly common in a country already known for its high crime rates.
On Saturday night, South African police said at least 10 people were killed at a shisanyama — a common kind of local restaurant selling barbecued meat — near Cape Town, while eleven others were injured.
The same night, near the commercial capital Johannesburg, 17 people were killed when a group of men with AK-47s burst into a township tavern where people were drinking.
The perpetrators "allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident," police said in a statement.
Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.
Earlier in the week, another mass shooting occurred in the coastal city of Durban. Police said 11 people, including a pregnant woman, were killed on Tuesday by multiple gunmen in an attack on a house party.
A motive for that crime was also unclear, but several people at the house were known to authorities as part of investigations into criminal activity.
Illegal guns are common in South Africa, where mass shooting events are usually linked to gangs and organized crime, sometimes surrounding activities involving illegal gold miners known as "zama-zamas."
In June, in another mass shooting, 12 people were killed when gunmen stormed an informal settlement in Johannesburg, where people live in tin shacks without access to running water and electricity. That shooting was blamed on turf wars between zama-zamas.
At the scene, NPR saw pools of blood under a snooker table in a makeshift bar roped off with police tape and traumatized residents described their fear when they heard the gunshots.
"I hid under my bed," said Angela Mopayi, 54, at the time, "I couldn't breathe, I couldn't do anything, I thought I was dying."
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, averaging 60 a day. But even so, the number of mass shootings has become a national crisis.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development," and deployed the army in some of the worst-affected areas.
President Trump has also been vocal about crime in South Africa since returning to office, but he has focused on the murders of white people on farms. While these do occur, official statistics show the vast majority of victims of crime are poor Black people.
And they are often also women. This month South Africans have been protesting amid a spate of brutal femicides in Johannesburg. On Saturday a tenth woman's body was discovered, despite police promises to crack down on gender-based violence.
South Africans head to the polls in November for local elections in which crime is expected to be a key issue.

articles.title_orig: Northern Ireland protesters block Orange Order march in Portadown
articles.title_zh: Northern Ireland protesters block Orange Order march in Portadown
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of protesters have blocked a route into the Catholic area of a Northern Irish town that a Protestant organisation was due to march down.
Northern Ireland’s High Court permitted the Protestant Orange Order organisation to march through a mainly Catholic area in the town of Portadown on Sunday for the first time in 28 years, reviving one of the region’s most contentious marching disputes.
The court rejected a final attempt by residents to stop the parade from passing through the Garvaghy Road, after Northern Ireland’s Court of Appeal overturned a temporary injunction granted on Saturday.
Thousands of people, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill of the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein and the party’s ‌leader, Mary Lou McDonald, gathered on the road to protest against the decision.
“This is madness,” McDonald told reporters shortly after 8am (07:00 GMT) when the march was due to begin. “This, in fact, is primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.
“This is a ⁠dignified and united community, and they are absolutely determined that ⁠they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”
McDonald and O’Neill urged the British government and police to intervene to stop the parade. O’Neill said she ⁠had spoken to Britain’s minister for the region and the Irish government.
Police vans parked nearby had earlier played out ⁠a warning that anyone taking part in the protest ⁠was committing a criminal offence.
A small group of Orange Order members wearing traditional silk orange sashes and black bowler hats gathered in another part of the town, a picture posted on X by Democratic Unionist Party ‌(DUP) lawmaker Carla Lockhart showed.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm, saying there have been “big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards”.
Jon Boutcher, the head of Northern Ireland police, called for “those with influence to encourage people to comply with the law”, referring to the protest blocking the Garvaghy Road. He said there have been no signs of violence or disorder.
“Police are engaging and working with all parties and will continue to do so. It is incumbent on us all to come together at times like this to do all we can to preserve a peaceful Northern Ireland.”
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, from the DUP, which supports Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, said on Sunday that threats of violence were unacceptable. “No one in Northern Ireland wants violence or disorder,” she added.
The Irish government said it was “very concerned” about the situation and that its priority was to avoid “a return to the divisions of the past”.
The Orange Order is a Protestant organisation closely associated with unionism, the political tradition that favours Northern Ireland remaining in the UK.
The Parades Commission, the independent body that rules on disputed marches in Northern Ireland, approved Sunday’s procession with a 35-person limit, barred bands and accompanying supporters, and required the march to finish by 9:30am (08:30 GMT).
The dispute over the Drumcree parade and Garvaghy Road became one of the most bitter marching confrontations of the “Troubles”, the decades-long conflict over Northern Ireland’s political status that largely ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
Repeated attempts by the Orange Order to return from Drumcree Parish Church along Garvaghy Road triggered protests, violence and major security operations during the 1990s.

Fresh off leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship in 53 years, Jalen Brunson took another victory lap at Studio 8H. The NBA point guard hosted the Season 52 premiere of Saturday Night Live alongside musical guest Katseye. It was Brunson's first time hosting SNL .
Although Brunson was presented with the key to the city after the Knicks' big win, he found there was one door that key didn't unlock — and it just so happened to lead to the SNL stage:
Here are the best moments from Brunson's SNL debut:
El Niño can't stop President Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson) from visiting his best friend (at least to him), New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (Ramy Youssef). While the mayor has a lot of important work ahead of him, Trump has nothing but time on his hands to cut it up with his favorite public official, whose relationship Trump likens to "one of those unlikely animal friendships." Also braving the weather is the president's obsessive, rain-soaked assistant Natalie Harp (Ashley Padilla), who vows to end Zohran if the mayor hurts Trump. Desperate to get $11 billion for a new housing project, Mamdani promises to follow Trump back on Instagram (if only real life lawmaking were so easy).
Jalen Brunson begins by promising to host SNL the same way he played an NBA playoff game: by being absolutely terrible for three quarters before pulling off a victory in the end. For Brunson, the most satisfactory thing about bringing the New York Knicks their first NBA championship since 1973 is proving all of his haters wrong, including ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith (Kenan Thompson), who shows up to publicly apologize. Brunson then takes questions from the audience, which happens to include fellow Knicks players Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, and Josh Hart, all of whom take to the stage to rapturous applause from the New York audience.
Brunson pokes fun at his basketball skills as Darius, an office worker who has trouble throwing a fast food wrapper into the waste basket. His co-workers (Mikey Day, Johnson, Ben Marshall, and Sarah Sherman) become increasingly embarrassed as he unsuccessfully throws one wrapper onto the floor after another. Turns out Darius is actually Brunson, who has always dreamed of working a menial job yet can't stop until he finally makes a basket. As Brunson often does in a real NBA game, he finally scores a goal.
When nerdy Brunson shows up at the high school gym, no one wants him to join the basketball team except for Jeremy Culhane, who loves to sing and dance as much as he loves shooting hoops. Unfortunately for Culhane, Brunson is better at balling than he looks, and frequently uses his teammates head as a bounce board. Culhane decides to give up basketball and audition for the high school musical instead, which is perfect considering he's fallen in love with classmate Veronika Slowikowska. Turns out Brunson is a pretty good singer, too, and steals poor Jeremy's girlfriend away from him with a love song.
Tucker Carlson is back at the Update desk to chat this summer's blockbuster hits pic.twitter.com/TimHhJ3SAp
Conservative commentator Tucker Carlson (Culhane) stops by the Weekend Update desk to comment on this summers record-breaking box office, including Spider-Man: Brand New Day, or as he likes to call it, "Brand New Gender" ("Spider- they ?"). He also has harsh words for breakout hit Obsession, decrying that "the left's idea of a horror movie is a woman forced to love a man." And let's not forget Toy Story 5, which tells kids, "You've got a friend in me, and his name is... Woody?"
Brunson is the first host for Saturday Night Live 's 52nd season. Next up on the SNL stage will be Dakota Johnson (with musical guest Turnstile) on Oct. 3; Shane Gillis (with musical guest Rosalía) on Oct. 10; and Inde Navarrette (with musical guest Gracie Abrams) on Oct. 31. SNL just won another Emmy in September, bringing its record-holding total to 114.
SNL added two new featured players to its roster for Season 52: Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter. All of the Season 51 cast members are returning except for Chloe Fineman (plus Bowen Yang, who departed after the Christmas episode). Ashley Padilla and Jane Wickline have been promoted to repertory players this season.

For years, residents of a Southern California beach town could walk a mile along a stretch of cream-colored sand while ocean waves lapped at their feet. That journey has now been cut short.
San Clemente, recognized for nearly a century as a "Spanish village by the sea," is losing its shoreline to erosion. Rising seas and crashing waves have bisected the city's picturesque North Beach, while eroding bluffs threaten waterfront homes and have repeatedly forced the closure of a passenger train route considered the second busiest in the country.
It is one of numerous California coastal communities confronting the effects of sea level rise. Nearly a decade ago, scientists forecast that more than half of Southern California ’s beaches could significantly erode by 2100, radically altering how people live and recreate along the state’s famed coast.
"The constant pressure is sea level rise," said Sean Vitousek, research oceanographer with the U.S. Geological Survey. "It is going to keep rising, and rising, and the beaches will retreat landward."
Following years of erosion, California is preparing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Niño, a temporary warming in parts of the equatorial Pacific that warps weather worldwide. Already this year, seawater flooded residences in Long Beach near Los Angeles during a hurricane-driven storm surge, and the town of Pacifica south of San Francisco closed its cracked concrete pier. A recent study indicated that El Niño events are strengthening due to human-caused climate change.
In San Clemente, a town of 62,000 people, urban development has restricted the flow of sediment that historically replenished local beaches, while warmer waters drive waves higher and further ashore. The challenge has led residents of the largely Republican city to consider taxing themselves for beach restoration. A measure adding a 1% sales tax to fund wildfire protection and sand replenishment is on the November ballot.
Over the past five years, the rail line operating along the coast for more than a century has faced recurring closures due to encroaching surf on one side and fragile bluffs on the other. The 7-mile (11-kilometer) segment belongs to a 351-mile (565-kilometer) passenger rail corridor connecting San Diego with Los Angeles County's major port complex and San Luis Obispo. It is also used by freight and the military.
Transportation officials have reinforced the tracks to ensure passenger safety by laying down rock. But as waves slam against the rocks, they sweep more sand offshore and accelerate erosion that will eventually threaten the rail line again.
Locals say the erosion is dramatically altering their community.
"We've lost our walkable beach," said Cameron Cosgrove, a San Clemente resident who wrote the tax measure. "It used to be you could come to North Beach, walk the beach trail, or on the beach to the pier and actually all the way down to the south end of town. Can’t do either anymore."
City and transit officials agree more sand is needed and note that coastal communities, including surf hub Huntington Beach, have nourished their beaches for years. Opponents of the measure want sand — but not the tax — and argue San Clemente should work with other communities on a regional approach.
"Fighting Mother Nature is very expensive," said City Councilman Zhen Wu, who opposes the measure.
City Manager Andy Hall said San Clemente faces a sand deficit of about 3 million cubic yards. Getting that much sand to the beach is no easy task, he said, adding that trucking it would require 300,000 trips.
Darrell Johnson, chief executive of the Orange County Transportation Authority, said a challenge has been getting state permits for more sand. He hopes California's recent emergency declaration ahead of El Niño will speed up the process. In the long run, Johnson said officials will study moving trains inland — an idea previously deemed too costly. A third option is to halt the line, he said.
"If we can’t figure out how to shore up properly in a way that is long-term in nature, and we can't figure out how to relocate, I think that is a question that’s going to have to be asked," Johnson said. "'What happens to passenger rail? What happens to freight?'"
Further south, transportation officials have been working to stabilize coastal bluffs to shore up the rail line in the community of Del Mar. The plan is to eventually move the tracks, but officials have not decided where.
Charlie Fox, a 56-year-old San Clemente resident and marine meteorologist, said sand provides a critical buffer between whatever structures — train tracks, homes, lifeguard headquarters — are built along the coast. The lifelong surfer said sand also helps waves roll gently onshore, creating a steady wave break for surfing.
On a recent morning, surfers bobbed in the water off North Beach, not far from the rocky structure shoring up the train tracks by the sea.
"When you see those rocks, that's them attempting to fight the ocean," Fox said. "That is a futile endeavor."
"The ocean wins," he added. "Ocean always eventually wins."

President Donald Trump appeared to intensify his irritation with GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar on Saturday evening after reposting a series of social media attacks on the congresswoman who made waves last week for breaking with him on his immigration tactics.
The president shared in quick succession on Truth Social at least 14 posts from other users critical of Salazar, who is facing a tough reelection race in Florida as Republicans’ midterm fortunes decline.
“She is nothing but a back stabber. I’m glad the Latino support hasn’t wavered,” one user wrote in a post shared by Trump.
Another user slammed the congresswoman: “She wants amnesty for the ppl how criminally crossed our borders defying our laws.”
“So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar,” different user said .
The GOP stampede away from Trump is growing — including in pretty red districts
CNN reached out to the White House and Salazar’s office and reelection campaign for comment on the reposts.
Salazar, who represents a heavily Hispanic district, drew Trump’s ire last week after she broke with the president in a new ad ahead of the midterms. The congresswoman addresses Trump directly in the ad, speaking straight to the camera as she says, “some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.”
Salazar points to statistics she said show that 50% of the people detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in July “had no criminal record.”
Following the ad’s release, Trump confirmed in response to a question from a reporter that he had seen the ad and still backed the Florida congresswoman, even though he did not share her view.
“I disagree with her,” Trump said in the Oval Office. He claimed that Salazar “got a little bit soft on the border” and wouldn’t have won without his endorsement.

Salazar told “Face The Nation” that she had a “very good conversation” with the president after releasing the campaign ad and characterized Trump as “very receptive” to her warning that Hispanic voters feel “betrayed” ahead of the midterm election.
The congresswoman’s ad comes as ICE increased immigration arrests nationwide over the summer. In August, for example, ICE took around 51,000 people into custody, setting a new high under the second Trump administration. The previous high had been set the month prior when the agency took more than 46,000 people into custody in July.

articles.title_zh: MLB, White House discuss playing game at national park
articles.content_orig:
Major League Baseball has played games in a cornfield, a NASCAR speedway and historic ballparks. Now, the league is apparently wondering whether it can add a national park to the list.
MLB approached the Trump administration about holding a regular-season game in a national park, and National Park Service Deputy Director Frank Lands recently visited Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming to examine three potential locations for a temporary baseball facility, The Washington Post reported.
The idea remains preliminary. No site has been selected and no permits have been issued. The White House stressed that MLB â not President Donald Trump or his administration â proposed the concept.
âThis is not a Presidential directive, nor is it being directed by the White House,â the White House told the Post.
For MLB, playing somewhere unexpected has increasingly become part of the schedule. In addition to international games in England, Australia, Japan, South Korea and Mexico, the league has staged games at Iowaâs âField of Dreamsâ site, historic Rickwood Field and Bristol Motor Speedway, where a temporary baseball field was constructed inside the NASCAR track.
Turning Grand Teton into the next destination could be considerably more complicated.
Hosting tens of thousands of baseball fans inside a national park could require substantial temporary infrastructure beyond the field itself, including facilities for spectators and players, broadcast crews, security, sanitation and emergency services â not to mention getting thousands of people to and from the site.
Those demands could run into Grand Tetonâs rules for special events. Events cannot alter the movement of visitors, wildlife or traffic, close roads or trails, or take place in designated wilderness areas. Commercial logos, banners and tent-like structures are also prohibited.
At least one location examined by Lands is reportedly already-disturbed land used for storage rather than untouched parkland. Conservation advocates have nevertheless raised concerns about the environmental impact and precedent of staging a major professional sporting event inside a national park.

articles.content_orig:
Grassroots organizer Yasmin Radjy on the Democratic ground game leading into the midterm elections
I n the run-up to the US midterm elections , Swing Left – a grassroots political group focused on electing Democrats to office – has spent time canvassing in dozens of districts across the country to hear from hundreds of thousands of voters.
Now, with fewer than 40 days until the US midterm elections, the group’s executive director, Yasmin Radjy, sets out what she feels Democrats have been getting right and wrong this election cycle, and why these races are vital for the party’s future control of the US Congress in the years to come.
We are now five weeks out. What do you feel have been, and will continue to be, the defining issues of these midterm races?
Yasmin Radjy : The two things head and shoulders above everything else that we’re hearing about: one is a feeling like the system is broken , and soon after that are various issues around cost of living. The two are often related, but there are very few conversations where one or both of those issues are not coming up. Everyone’s gotten the memo that we need to talk about affordability. I don’t think there’s a Republican or a Democrat who’s not aware of that. The candidates who are really standing out this cycle again across the ideological spectrum, from Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan] to Mary Peltola [in Alaska]. And on the House map, Paige Cognetti [in Pennsylvania], to Amish Shah [in Arizona]. They are connecting those dots in a way that is specific and that is also mirroring the nature of those districts.
What do you think the party needs to focus on to regain trust, and establish a clear sense of identity with voters moving forward – particularly after 2024?
We have to follow up with people when they express urgency around the very real and material concerns that they have. When they express disappointment, we can’t pretend like everything is going great. We also need to acknowledge that a lot of the things we’ve been doing aren’t working. That requires having tough, not just conversations, but introspection, and openness to trying new things, testing new things and taking bigger, riskier swings than we’re accustomed to.
On one of the must-win races you mentioned – the open Senate seat in Michigan – what do you feel voters are responding to with a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed? What do you think he needs to do in order to win over voters in that state that Trump won?
I think something he is modeling is a “talk to everybody and engage with everyone” approach, not just talk to the people who already agree with you. I think he really won his primary because of organizing. In terms of the issues and themes in Michigan, what we’re hearing is very similar to elsewhere with subtle differences: both parties suck, and no politician cares about that voter, their community and people like them. That is ubiquitous. What he is able to speak compellingly on with a lot of authority is his feeling like the system is broken, and he is doing a good job of tying that to affordability and a whole host of other issues.
I’m curious what you think might be the biggest obstacle for Democrats in this cycle? What could be getting in the party’s way?
One is that we continue to not have a sufficiently clear answer, for a time when the winds are not blowing in our direction, of what Democrats stand for besides being anti-Trump. We need to start answering that now – and it’s OK if that answer has shades of difference in Michigan, Alaska and North Carolina. The second piece is we cannot assume our base will be with us again because of anti-Trump sentiment in a way that can sustain durable power.
Something under-discussed that keeps me up at night is if we are not building long-term, durable power, by 2030 we are going to wake up to an election where, if we don’t have power in the states, we will not be able to win congressional majorities because of how bad redistricting will look. Population shifts are clear in California and New York – two big blue states essential for presidential math – and they will be losing electoral college votes starting in 2030. Texas and Florida are the inverse – they are going to gain power. If we don’t treat the midterms as our most important moment to build infrastructure while there’s money pouring in, while there’s energy to have a shot at winning tough Republican seats in a way we can sustain, we are going to lose without question in the future, because we will have squandered an opportunity.
I want to discuss the concerns about progressives, from establishment Democrats. What’s your response to those in the coalition who question whether these progressive candidates have a real shot in battlegrounds that the party wants to either retain or flip?
We have members who are Democratic Socialists of America members. We have members who think DSA is a huge threat to democracy – we’ve got the full gamut. Our perspective is that the fixation on ideology and the DSA-versus-centrist divide is a completely false binary. We need to win a majority, and there is a level of pragmatism among the grassroots that is underappreciated. The binary will crumble, not because it doesn’t exist in our institutions, but because that’s not how voters are . We talk to voters every day who might be DSA-aligned on healthcare and Blue Dog-aligned on the border, and it’s the same person. If we lead with genuine curiosity and openness to listening to voters, we immediately see that voters are idiosyncratic, strange and full of contradictions because they’re human.
Linked to this, I’m thinking about James Talarico [the Democratic nominee for the US Senate seat in Texas] and Rob Sand [the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa]. They are showing a pivot in their messaging, particularly when it comes to trans rights. Do you feel that is a necessary strategy right now to court those swing voters, independents and moderates in newly competitive battleground states?
I think when you go out and really talk to people, specifically on the issue of trans rights, most Americans want trans people to have rights – and the areas of discomfort range from lack of knowledge. Their worldview on trans issues is curated by Fox News, so there is an information gap. Most voters, including many Democrats, have complicated feelings about the trans people in sports issue. The answer is not to start repeating Fox News talking points. The way to talk about these issues – and this is what the data shows – is to break down the pieces: all Americans want every American to have a certain set of freedoms. The trans and sports issue is complicated, and it is not really a decision for governments, it’s a decision for the leagues.
I think Sarah McBride is a perfect example of this – leading with grace, recognizing that changing hearts and minds takes time, and that people use clunky language along the way.
Looking ahead, do you think Democrats are doing enough to respond to Donald Trump’s efforts to undermine elections in this cycle in particular?
I would say there is an asymmetric investment in election protection right now. And that asymmetric investment is on the litigation front, it is on the donor-organizing and on the grassroots-organizing fronts. And I feel really confident and really relieved, candidly, that the amount of investment of time, talent and strategy has been placed on that. The flip side is the progressive ecosystem, overall, has not invested as much in the actual act of winning the election, and there is nothing more important for election protection than winning each competitive race by a big enough margin that Trump doesn’t have the incentive to try any kind of funny business. We are not where we should be in some of the most competitive races in the country in terms of dollars invested and volunteers ready to help that candidate, and to me, that is the most essential ingredient to election protection.

WASHINGTON — A divided Supreme Court has cleared the way for President Trump to finish building his new White House ballroom with mostly private money and without approval from Congress.
By a 5-4 vote, the justices granted an emergency appeal from Trump and his lawyers on Monday, setting aside a judge’s order that would stop the construction.
But Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. dissented, along with the court’s three liberals.
Roberts said the construction project was “likely unlawful” and should not be allowed to continue.
“The White House is not just any building ... when it comes to historic preservation,” Roberts wrote. “Winston Churchill once remarked that ‘[w]e shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.’ All the more reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House.”
The outcome turned on the standing of the plaintiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation and its members.
The conservative majority pointed to Alison Hoagland, one of its members, who said she lives in Washington, walks by the White House about once a month and said she found the “scale,” “height” and “massing” of the huge ballroom to be distasteful.
“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury,” the unsigned order said.
Trump has responded to growing legal and political obstacles to his ballroom, arch and other projects by attempting to force approvals through faster than opponents can challenge them.
It is a major victory for Trump, whose ballroom project has become a signature effort of his second term and a political lightning rod in Washington, where Republicans have refused to fund it with public money.
Trump celebrated the victory with a post on social media, declaring the venue would now be built “without any further contingency, doubt, or threat.”
“We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of.”
The massive new structure, set to dwarf the historic White House mansion, is the president’s singular vision — one of a string of aesthetic projects Trump has pursued in a feverish effort to cement his legacy by putting his personal stamp on the nation’s capital.
But preservationists and architects have criticized the proposed ballroom as a garish, rushed project that ignored the input of experts. The president has personally overruled his own chosen architects after being told the building would overwhelm the executive complex.
Democrats have seized on the president’s fixation on the ballroom as a symbol of vanity and detachment from the concerns of everyday Americans heading into November’s midterm elections.
According to recent polls, a bipartisan majority of voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy and say the country is facing an affordability crisis. The ballroom is projected to cost more than $400 million, excluding the undisclosed cost of underground security upgrades.
Trump’s three appointees — Justices Neil M. Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — joined conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito in an unsigned opinion ruling for the president.
The conservative majority also said Trump and his appointees had stressed the new ballroom was needed for national security and said the lower courts judges should not have interfered.
California officials stressed that the court’s ruling does not allow final implementation of the new rules requested by Trump.
Administration officials have argued that an underground “integrated military complex” was the heart of the project and that the ballroom would merely be sit top of the facility “vitally required by national security.”
The decision is not a final ruling, but it gives a green light to Trump’s go-it-alone approach, which is in keeping with his history as a hotel builder.
He believed the White House needed a grand ballroom that could seat hundreds of dignitaries. Acting on his own, he ordered the East Wing torn down in October to make room of his larger ballroom.
He also said most of the project would be paid for by private donations.
But the Constitution gave Congress the power to manage property belonging to the United States. A 1912 law says new buildings “shall not erected ... on public grounds within the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”
Trump chose to ignore the law and did not seek approval from Congress, which is led by Republicans.
The Republican president’s lawyers had asked the justices to reconsider their refusal to hear his appeal. The court denied Trump’s petition along with several others.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued in December, contending Trump was a “temporary tenant, not the owner” of the White House.
U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ruled Trump had no authority to build a ballroom on the White House grounds without the approval of Congress, and he ordered a halt to the above-ground construction.
The District of Columbia Circuit Court affirmed his decision by a 2-1 vote.
“Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People’s House — to fit a particular President’s desires,” wrote Judge Patricia Millett for the appeals court.
Trump’s lawyers sent a fast-track appeal to the Supreme Court on Aug. 14.
The court’s majority allowed Trump to fend off the legal challenge by concluding the historic preservationists could not show they were harmed by  the huge new ballroom.

Tennessee Volunteers fans told OutKick's Trey Wallace they're excited for President Donald Trump to attend a key SEC matchup against the Texas Longhorns on Saturday, and they left with their final score predictions.
KNOXVILLE, TN - It only took four weeks of action to immerse ourselves in the madness of college football, with upsets and teams already up against the ropes heading into the month of October.
Are schools already looking to make changes at the head coaching position? Sure, and some leaders might end up making the decision pretty easy for their bosses.

But what we witnessed on Saturday will go down as one of the wildest weekends of this early season, and there will be ramifications.
ARCH MANNING REVELS IN CIGAR SMOKE: TEXAS LEAVES NEYLAND WITH WIN—AND A WARNING FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL
Heck, Texas led Tennessee by ten points late in the fourth quarter, but had to withstand a last minute drive by the Vols to get out of Knoxville with the win. There wasn’t even a touchdown pass thrown by Arch Manning on Saturday, but the defense ended up with over ten sacks on Vols quarterback Faizon Brandon, in what felt like a Will Muschamp defensive revival.
We're only getting started on this wild weekend in college football.
Oregon lost quarterback Dante Moore to a head injury in the first half, thanks to a dirty hit. But, that did not end their hopes of beating USC. Two weeks after losing to Oklahoma State, the Ducks rolled into Southern Cal and once again left Trojan fans wondering when Lincoln Riley was going to win a few meaningful games.
Quarterback Dylan Raiola of the Oregon Ducks throws the ball in the first half against the USC Trojans at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Sept. 26, 2026, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Getty Images)
We don't know when Moore will return, but backup Dylan Raiola took the reigns on Saturday night and never looked back. Throwing for over 280 yards against USC, this might be the start of Raiola's redemption tour, at least until Dante Moore returns.
But, a massive 41-27 win for the Ducks have put their season back on track, while USC fans are left wondering what else Lincoln Riley feels like putting them through.
Who would of thought before the season started that Oklahoma would already be regretting that contract extension for Brent Venables. But just four games into the 2026 season, the Sooners have a major problem on their hands, thanks in part to the 41-13 drumming by the Georgia Bulldogs on Saturday afternoon in Athens.
Oh, and if you were wondering whether Ole Miss was walking into a trap this week in Gainesville after defeating LSU last weekend, I think that would be disrespecting what Jon Sumrall is doing with the Florida Gators.
A 52-28 loss on the road brought the Rebels back down to reality, with Pete Golding having to regroup his team this week after a rollercoaster two-week stretch. But make no mistake about it, the Florida Gators look nothing like the team we witnessed during the Billy Napier era.
FLORIDA DROPS IMPRESSIVE OFFENSIVE PERFORMANCE TO PULL OFF MASSIVE WIN OVER NO. 4 OLE MISS
Florida Gators head coach Jon Sumrall looks on during the second half of a game against the Ole Miss Rebels at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium in Gainesville, Fla., on Sept. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)
And, speaking of teams we thought could get things back on track in 2026, South Carolina has itself a major problem moving forward under head coach Shane Beamer. Not only were they beaten 49-18 by Alabama, the Gamecocks feel like a rudderless ship, with such high expectations for quarterback LaNorris Sellers before the season began.
Now? The Gamecocks lost their seventh-straight SEC game, and it doesn’t look any better moving forward.
Well, this is only going to make things worse in Columbia for Beamer, who had spent a good chunk of money to keep a number of stars from hitting the portal, like Dylan Stewart.
Is Kamario Taylor going to end up being the catalyst that brings Mississippi State back to college football relevance? Well, he already has, and looks darn good in the process.
The 24th ranked Bulldogs defeated No. 19 Missouri, winning their first ranked game in over a decade, with Taylor passing for over 350 yards on the night.
Look out, Alabama. The Bulldogs are waiting next week in Starkville. \
Kamario Taylor No. 1 of the Mississippi State Bulldogs warms up before the game at Davis Wade Stadium in Starkville, Miss., on Sept. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)
An Iowa Hawkeyes touchdown with only one second left on the clock left Michigan fans stunned , probably the same way Western Michigan fans felt during the week-one controversy that allowed the Wolverines to escape with a win.
Three weeks later, it was Kirk Ferentz who delivered the karma like a Taylor Swift single, which had college football fans outside of the state chuckling I'd imagine.
No, this looks nothing like a team that should be paying its quarterback Bryce Underwood over $3 million per season. In reality, this feels like a squad headed for a December bowl game, and nowhere near the Big Ten championship. At this point, maybe it would be wise for Michigan fans to start preparing for the Ohio State game to end the season, and not get their hopes up every weekend.
That win against Oklahoma also looks even worse by the week.
Head coach Kirk Ferentz of the Iowa Hawkeyes shakes hands with Kyle Whittingham of the Michigan Wolverines after Iowa's 20-19 win at Michigan Stadium on Sept. 26, 2026, in Ann Arbor, Mich. (Getty Images)
So, you thought Lane Kiffin would just go quiet into the night after losing to his former team last week in Oxford?
Not only did LSU take out their frustration on Texas A&M, but they made it look easy in the 38-6 win. Sam Leavitt carved up the Aggies secondary, while Kiffin found himself running down the sidelines celebrating a fourth-down trick play that turned into a touchdown.
Simply put, the Tigers made Mike Elko's squad look like a mediocre SEC team without much hope moving forward. We should probably go ahead and count the Aggies out of making the College Football Playoff, while LSU looks to have gotten the 'Lane Train' back on the tracks in Baton Rouge.
Head coach Lane Kiffin of the Louisiana State Tigers takes the field before a game against the Mississippi Rebels at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium in Oxford, Miss., on Sept. 19, 2026. (Getty Images)
Can someone explain to me how Louisville could lose at home to Wake Forest 30-27, with this squad battling for 'surprise' team of the season out of the ACC?
Well, that went up in smoke inside their own stadium.
Oh, and how could we not mention the job Luke Fickell did on Saturday, leading his Wisconsin Badgers into Happy Valley and leaving with the 24-20 win that left folks in State College shocked. People forget that Fickell didn’t just wake up and turn into a bad coach. He just hasn’t had the necessary resources in Madison.
Head coach Luke Fickell of the Wisconsin Badgers shakes hands with head coach Matt Campbell of the Penn State Nittany Lions after the game at Beaver Stadium on Sept. 26, 2026, in State College, Pa. (Getty Images)
He still might not have everything he needs to rebuild the Wisconsin football team, but they darn sure made Penn State pay for potentially looking past the Badgers.
Week four of the college football season delivered, which will setup a wild start to the month of October.

UFC fighter Raoni Barcelos was hospitalized at a Level 1 trauma center in the aftermath of Saturday's loss to Raul Rosas Jr.
UFC released a statement that said Barcelos was "stable, alert and responsive, with full movement" after undergoing a CT scan.
As ESPN's Jeff Wagenheim described, Barcelos "appeared to lose consciousness after a fifth-round takedown and was carried from the cage on a stretcher" at the end of the UFC Fight Night matchup in Las Vegas.
Wagenheim noted Barcelos' coach, Davi Ramos, provided an update on Saturday as well and said, "everything is fine, everyone can stay calm."
As for the fight itself, Rosas was trailing heading into the final round but was more aggressive toward the end. After he slammed Barcelos to the mat, the referee stopped the fight when it seemed as if the 39-year-old was unconscious.
Rosas, who became the youngest fighter to ever sign with UFC at 17 years old in 2022, has now won six fights in a row.
However, he was focused on his opponent in the aftermath as well.
"I want everybody tonight to please pray for Raoni Barcelos," he said in his postfight interview to the crowd. "Man, he's a warrior. It takes two to tango."
UFC's statement said Barcelos "will remain under medical supervision. We will provide updates on his condition as they become available."

The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.
Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL'
“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”
Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.
“Can you foul out of ‘SNL’?” Towns asked.
In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson played a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”
It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with an over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.
The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than Culhane’s character’s. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed Season 2 of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

Raoni Barcelos lost a UFC main event fight to Raul Rosas Jr. in Las Vegas
The UFC Vegas 121 main event clash between Raoni Barcelos and Raul Rosas Jr. ended in scary fashion in the fifth round when the Brazilian bantamweight went unconscious for apparent no reason during a clinch exchange. Barcelos was rushed to the hospital for exams after the bout, and his head coach Davi Ramos shared on social media he is now back to his senses.
The UFC released a statement hours after the incident to confirm Barcelos was transported to a Level 1 trauma center for evaluation and was “stable, alert and responsive, with full movement” after a “CT scan and comprehensive assessment” were conducted.
“Raoni is doing well,” Ramos said in Portuguese on a video posted on social media. “He has all his senses, he’s moving his leg, his arm, his hand, he’s conscious, he’s talking, everything is fine with him. He’s undergoing some tests, and pretty soon he’ll be here to talk to you guys.”
“I just wanted to let you know so you can all stay calm,” he continued. “Keep praying for him. He’s undergoing all the tests that are standard in a situation like this. He’ll have to rest because of what happened, but God willing, everything will be fine. He’ll be here with us soon and he’ll be talking to you guys. Thank you to everyone who’s been sending messages, positive energy, praying and keeping all of us in your prayers.”
Barcelos was up in all three scorecards going into the final round, including a 10-8 in round four for one of the judges, meaning he was a little over three minutes away from a decision victory. The loss snapped what would be his sixth straight victory in the UFC.
“We had a great fight,” Ramos said. “We practice a sport that we can’t predict, unfortunately, but we know for sure that we were doing our best. Raoni is a warrior, a phenomenal fighter, and he showed you that with all the technique he has, all the skill and heart he has. He showed everything about where he wants to go, where we all want to go, with all the work we’ve been putting in. Congratulations to him, and thank you all for the messages. Keep praying for him, and pretty soon he’ll be back here with us to put on another great show.”
Update: Ramos also shared a statement from Barcelos’ doctor, Dr. Gustavo Medeiros.
“I’m here with this message to bring some good news and reassurance to everyone who has been sending messages to Raoni’s team and family. As everyone knows, Raoni suffered a sudden illness during the fight and was initially hospitalized as a precaution. At this moment, he is lucid and oriented. I’m in direct contact with our team there in the United States, in Las Vegas, so I’m very well informed about the situation. He is lucid and oriented at this moment, and he is hospitalized strictly as a matter of protocol. He needs to remain under observation for a few days to assess his condition and make sure that everything remains stable and that he continues to do well. … He is doing well, and he’ll be back with you soon, much stronger.”

articles.title_orig: From professor to patient: One man's journey on the frontier of lung cancer treatment
articles.title_zh: From professor to patient: One man's journey on the frontier of lung cancer treatment
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Bryant Lin teaches a lung cancer class in fall 2024. He says he was very nervous to teach the first class and share his story. The Lin family hide caption
Stanford medical professor Bryant Lin founded the school's Center for Asian Health Research and Education , advocating for better lung cancer screening in particular. Then two years ago Lin became a Stage IV patient of the very disease he long crusaded against.
"Super ironic that I would be co-leading the center that supports research and education in this disease, and I get diagnosed myself," he says.
Lin, who is a non-smoker, tells students he considers himself lucky — even hopeful: "I think the future is really bright, because we're creating all of these personalized, specialized precision therapeutics for lung cancer," he says."My hope is if we're not able to cure lung cancer, we can at least turn it into a chronic disease."
Notable improvements are shifting the prognosis for a disease once considered a death sentence. Much of the recent progress is so new, it is only starting to shift the statistics on survival. While the five-year survival rate across all stages of lung cancer has doubled in three decades, it still remains at a low 30%. (Stage of disease makes a huge difference; early, localized cancer survival rates over 5 years was 67% between 2015 and 2021.)
The genetics of lung cancers are very diverse and complex relative to other cancers, making it historically tricky to treat. One key technological development underlying many new treatments is the ability to identify, through genetic testing, the specific mutation driving a person's abnormal cell growth, according to UCLA oncologist and researcher Jonathan Goldman . "We can pick a drug that's really been developed for that type of cancer," he says.
Not only can that manage or even shrink tumors, because the drugs are better targeted, they also cause less collateral damage, making side effects typically more tolerable for patients.
"Survival used to be under a year, and now it's often several years and sometimes many years," Goldman says.
Whether it's breast, liver or lung cancer, targeting treatments by genetic subtype is far more effective than generalized treatments of the past, Goldman says, because the medicines are designed to focus their attack on specific mutated cells driving the abnormal growth. Since the medicines are targeted, they also tend to have fewer harsh side effects compared to chemotherapy.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
Tests to identify a patient's specific cancer subtype – a procedure called comprehensive genomic testing – are already available, and Goldman served as principal investigator on a recent study published in the New England Journal of Medicine , showing dramatic reductions in recurrence, when patients with rare subtypes receive targeted medicines as their first treatment.
However, access to such testing is spotty. Goldman says fewer than half of lung-cancer patients in the U.S. get their cancer genetically tested prior to treatment because that evaluation is not yet considered "standard of care." Plus, doctors themselves may not be aware it exists; Goldman says treatment technology is changing so rapidly, general oncologists may not be up-to-date on some of the most recent developments specific to lung cancer.
"The next step is not just these scientific discoveries, but learning how to implement these findings," he says. "We've proven time and time again how important and effective it is to get this testing done early so you can pick your best treatment first."
It was one of those relatively new targeted drugs, a daily pill called Tagrisso (or osimertinib), that professor-patient Bryant Lin initially began taking when he was first diagnosed in May 2024. Just three months prior to that, the Food and Drug Administration approved its use in combination with chemotherapy , based on data showing it lengthened survival.
"I am a beneficiary of years – of decades – of research," Lin says, noting how his treatment regimen has closely mapped with some of the most recent drug developments. "Since I've been diagnosed. It's quite amazing how quick – how rapid – our advances have been occurring."
Treatment is one thing; affording them is another. Even Lin, a patient with the unusual privilege of being a nationally known expert at an elite medical center, faces battles with insurance to get some of these new, expensive treatments covered. Insurers almost always require prior authorization for the treatments, or deny coverage for new drugs that haven't yet received expert endorsement as standard protocol. Lin says this happened for one of his $16,000 drugs, delaying his treatment at a critical time. He watches patients, too, fight similar battles over coverage.
"Oral drugs and the IV drugs — they're hundreds of thousands of dollars," he says. "I don't know too many people who could afford to pay out of pocket."
A year into his treatment, the initial targeted therapy Lin was taking stopped working. By then, regulators approved another drug combination – amivantamab and lazertinib – an antibody to activate the immune system, and a different pill targeting his specific mutation type, known as EGFR.
Dr. Bryant Lin receives a chemo infusion in the early days of his treatment in June 2024. The Lin family hide caption
Lin, who still teaches , travels, and advises the Susan Wojcicki Foundation for lung cancer, says these new therapies have given him both more life, and one of better quality. "My symptoms are really well controlled. I can live my life. I can speak. I don't think I've coughed once in our conversation."
What's more, there's a compounding effect with this kind of scientific progress, where recent breakthroughs with other genetically similar cancers may soon apply to lung cancer.
One promising area of potential crossover is with pancreatic cancer, which is driven by a gene in the same KRAS family that causes a sizable minority of lung cancers. One drug the FDA approved in August called Rasonque (generic name daraxonrasib), doubled survival for late-stage cancer patients to over 13 months in clinical trials – a rare victory against pancreatic cancer, a particularly stubborn form of the disease.
There are other promising drugs for pancreatic cancer that may eventually find application against lung cancer as well, including mRNA vaccines — custom designed to match the genetic profile of each individual's cancer. Researchers and companies say those show promise re-enlisting the immune system into fighting tumors.
"I've been investigating that for myself – personalized mRNA vaccine," Lin says.
Lin's professional focus remains on advocating for better modes and rates of screening, which remains at a stubbornly 18% among the high-risk patients for whom annual, low-dose CT scan screening (image tests) is the standard recommendation. But with screening, too, there is progress: AI imaging and increasingly sensitive blood tests may help detect, or even predict, formation of disease even years earlier.
Just as colorectal cancers can now be screened for using blood, stool and colonoscopy tests, Lin wants to see options besides the CT scan for lung cancer. Expanding these kinds of surveillance technologies could ultimately do more to reduce lung cancer deaths.
Lin himself is like a trapeze artist, grabbing hold from one treatment to the next. A fellow cancer patient told him: All he needs is to do is hang on. "He says, 'Hey, you only need to survive long enough until the next new treatment comes out' – and that's been the case for me," Lin says. His life of limbo involves balancing acts – as doctor and patient, as optimist and realist. "I'm hopeful," he says. "But, absolutely: The odds are against me."

Oops, something went wrong
For the better part of the last four years, Wall Street's bull market has been unstoppable. Aside from the short-lived tariff tantrum in April 2025 and a brief pullback associated with the Iran war earlier this year, the time-tested Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have all blasted to several record highs this year.
Catalysts have been abundant and include (but aren't limited to):
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
